Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Atiyya donnent les mêmes possibilités sans trancher. Ibn al-Qayyim, pour sa part, estime que le verset est une bonne nouvelle donnée au défunt à son départ de ce monde. Les commentateurs ne tranchent pas entre ces lectures, les présentant comme des sens que le contexte peut soutenir.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset achève la description des trois catégories d'hommes au moment de la mort et après. Il évoque ici le troisième groupe, celui des négateurs égarés. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi disent qu'ils auront un « nuzul », c'est-à-dire ce que l'on offre à l'hôte, qui est une eau bouillante parvenue à l'extrême de sa chaleur, et une « tasliya » dans la fournaise, c'est-à-dire être brûlé par le feu. Ibn 'Atiyya précise qu'il s'agit des infidèles, les gens de la gauche et de la direction défavorable, et que le nuzul est ce que l'on sert en premier à un visiteur, tandis que la tasliya désigne le contact direct avec le feu. Ibn Juzayy et al-Qurtubi identifient également ce groupe aux mécréants. Al-Razi remarque que la mention du démenti est placée ici en premier parce que le châtiment est lié à sa cause, contrairement à ce qui se trouve dans le verset cinquante et un. Al-Zamakhshari comprend le mot nuzul comme une ironie. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que cette rétribution est une certitude, « haqq al-yaqin ». Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi notent que certains rattachent ce sort au moment de l'agonie, et d'autres au Jour de la Résurrection. La sourate se termine par l'ordre de glorifier le nom de son Seigneur le Très Grand, et al-Qurtubi et Ibn 'Atiyya rapportent que le Prophète demanda de le réciter dans l'inclinaison, avec des divergences sur la chaîne de transmission de ce hadith.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset fait partie de la description du sort des hommes au moment de la mort. Il évoque le cas de ceux qui ont traité la vérité de mensonge et se sont égarés : leur « nuzul », c'est-à-dire ce que l'on offre à un hôte à son arrivée, est un « hamîm », une eau portée à une chaleur extrême, puis une « tasliyat jahîm », c'est-à-dire un enfoncement dans la fournaise et un brûlement par le feu. La plupart s'accordent à voir dans le mot « nuzul » une ironie : c'est une hospitalité offerte à ces gens sur le mode du dérisoire, et le « hamîm » est une eau d'une chaleur brûlante dont ils sont abreuvés. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir rapportent que la tasliya désigne l'introduction dans le feu, tandis qu'al-Qurtubi et d'autres la comprennent comme un séjour dans la fournaise et l'endurance de ses différents supplices. Certains, comme le rapporte al-Alusi, rattachent la scène à ce que le défunt ressent dans la tombe, la chaleur et la fumée du feu, d'autres la placent au jour de la résurrection. Ibn Kathir cite une hadith sur l'âme du défunt sur ce point, mais les autres commentateurs ne la mentionnent pas. Abu Hayyan note qu'Abu 'Amr lit « tasliyati » au génitif, la faisant dépendre de « hamîm », tandis que la lecture majoritaire la met au nominatif, en coordination avec « nuzul ». Ces divergences portent surtout sur le moment et la nature de ce tourment, non sur le sens général du verset.

Ce verset décrit le sort de ceux qui se trouvent à l'agonie selon leur rang. Les rapprochés, c'est-à-dire les premiers à la foi, reçoivent repos, bienfait et jardin de délices ; les gens de la droite reçoivent le salut, c'est-à-dire la sécurité contre le châtiment ; les négateurs égarés ont pour hospitalité une eau bouillante et l'entrée dans la fournaise. Les commentateurs expliquent que la taṣliya désigne le fait d'être brûlé ou plongé dans le feu, et que la Jahîm est un nom du feu.

La plupart des exégètes s'accordent à voir dans le verset une division des hommes en trois catégories au moment de la mort. En revanche, ils divergent sur le sens de le repos (rawḥ). Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir le comprennent comme un repos et une tranquillité, Ibn Kathir y ajoutant la miséricorde, la joie et la subsistance, tandis qu'Ibn al-Jawzi en recense six, dont la joie, le pardon et la délivrance de l'angoisse. Pour al-Hasan, le rayḥān est une plante odorante dans laquelle l'âme est rendue, alors que Mujahid et Ibn 'Abbas y voient la subsistance.

La lecture de (fa-rawḥun) avec une voyelle de pluriel est rapportée d'Aïcha, d'Ibn 'Abbas et d'al-Hasan, qui lui donne le sens de miséricorde. Quant au salut adressé aux gens de la droite, al-Tabari y voit une sauvegarde contre le châtiment, Ibn Kathir un salut des anges, et al-Razi estime que le discours peut s'adresser au Prophète pour le consoler. Ces explications sont présentées par les commentateurs comme convergentes, sans qu'un jugement définitif ne soit tranché.

Ce verset affirme que ce qui a été décrit dans la sourate al-Waqi'a, au sujet des états des hommes à la mort et dans l'au-delà, est la vérité certaine, la certitude absolue. Les commentateurs ont expliqué diversement la construction « haqq al-yaqin ». Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi y voient le sens de « la vérité issue de la certitude » ou « le récit certain ». Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Atiyya y voient une insistance destinée à renforcer le sens, comme on dit « c'est la certitude de la certitude », c'est-à-dire sa limite extrême. Al-Razi indique que la construction peut reposer sur un terme sous-entendu ou sur le sens de « parmi ». Quant à l'ordre « Glorifie le nom de ton Seigneur, le Grand », al-Tabari l'explique comme l'invocation des noms les plus beaux de Dieu, tandis qu'Ibn al-Jawzi et d'autres y voient la prière et l'évocation du Seigneur. Certains affirment que la particule « bi » est superflue. Ibn al-Jawzi et Ibn Kathir rapportent le hadith de 'Uqba ibn 'Amir qui recommande de réciter ce verset dans l'inclinaison (ruku'). Les commentateurs ne tranchent pas entre ces avis et les présentent comme des lectures possibles du texte.

Dans cette conclusion, Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète de glorifier le nom de son Seigneur le Très Grand, c'est-à-dire de Le déclarer exempt de tout ce qui ne convient pas à Sa majesté, après avoir affirmé que ce qui a été décrit sur le sort des trois catégories au moment de la mort et après celle-ci est la certitude vraie, sans doute aucun. Les exégètes s'accordent à voir dans ce verset une clôture de ce qui précède, et la glorification comme une exaltation et une louange de Dieu. Ils divergent sur la particule « bi » : beaucoup disent qu'elle est superflue et que le sens est « glorifie le nom de ton Seigneur », d'autres qu'elle marque l'accompagnement, c'est-à-dire glorifie-Le en invoquant Son nom, et d'autres qu'elle introduit le complément. Al-Tabari et d'autres rapportent que « le nom » peut désigner l'Essence divine. Quant à l'expression « vérité de la certitude », les grammairiens de Basra la rattachent à une ellipse, « la vérité de la chose certaine », tandis que les Kufiens y voient une apposition ou une annexion d'un terme à lui-même pour insister ; Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Mubarrad y voient une exagération. Qatada rapporte que Dieu ne laisse personne sans le mettre face à la certitude de ce Coran : le croyant en profite dans l'au-delà, tandis que l'incrédule la découvre trop tard. Plusieurs exégètes citent le hadith de 'Uqba ibn 'Amir selon lequel le Prophète ordonna de réciter ce verset dans l'inclinaison, ce qui a été retenu par les juristes pour la prière. Certains relient le passage à l'éloignement des propos des incrédules et à l'attachement à l'adoration et à l'invocation.
en: The opening verses declare that when the Event, called al-Waqi'a because its occurrence is certain, takes place, no one will be able to deny or reverse it, and it will bring low some peoples and raise others. The commentators agree that this refers to the Day of Resurrection. They differ on what causes it: Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to be the Blast or the final blow of the trumpet, while al-Suddi takes it to be the Hour itself, which truly arrives and is not denied. Most explain the word kadhiba as a verbal noun, like 'afiya or 'aqiba, meaning that there will be no return or reversal, as al-Tabari reports from Qatada. On the lowering and raising, Ibn Abbas and Ikrima say it means the voice makes both near and far hear it, whereas Qatada, Umar ibn al-Khattab and Muhammad ibn Ka'b say it means that God's enemies are lowered to the Fire and His friends raised to Paradise. All agree that the earth will shake violently and the mountains will be crushed like wet flour and then become scattered dust. The meaning of hiba' is debated: a sunbeam entering through a window, according to Mujahid and Ibn Abbas; the dust raised by animals, according to Ali; sparks from a fire, in another report from Ibn Abbas; or dried leaves blown by the wind, according to Qatada. The surah then divides people into three groups: the companions of the right, the companions of the left, and the foremost. The Quran exalts the first group with the phrase 'what are the companions of the right'. Ibn Kathir and most commentators hold that these categories frame the descriptions of Paradise and Hell that follow.

This verse affirms that when the Event comes, nothing can deny it: it is a certain and unavoidable reality. The commentators explain that it will abase some people and raise others, bringing God's enemies down to the Fire and lifting His friends to Paradise. Most agree that the word kadhiba is a verbal noun meaning denial or falsehood, like aqiba or afiya. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that nothing can turn it back or delay it, while Qatada adds that there is no return or retraction. Others, such as al-Kisa'i, understand that no one should deny it. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that no soul will lie at that moment, since every soul will believe. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the word could also describe a state or an account. As for lowering and raising, Ikrima, Qatada and al-Suddi see it as the cry reaching both the near and the far, or as the humbling of the arrogant and the exaltation of the weak. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi treat it as an image of the event's immense severity, God alone truly raising and abasing. The commentators then describe the quaking of the earth, the crumbling of the mountains into scattered dust, and the various readings of the word habaʾ, such as a sunbeam through a window, the dust of animals, or sparks from a fire. The overall meaning is that this day is certain and terrible, and that it will separate people according to their deeds.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Hour when it arrives: it "lowers" some people, who are cast down to the Fire, and "raises" others, who are lifted to the Garden. Most of them, including Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Sa'di, understand this as a recompense according to deeds rather than worldly rank. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and al-Hasan are reported to say that God's enemies are brought down to the Fire and His friends raised to the Garden. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, quoted by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, says it lowers those who were exalted in this world and raises those who were humbled.

Others take the meaning in a literal sense. 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and Muqatil say the Blast lowers its voice so the near can hear it and raises it so the far can hear it. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also see a picture of the terror of that day, when everything is upended, what is high is brought low and what is low is raised. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the lowering and raising are attributed figuratively to the moment in which they occur.

The commentators agree that the Hour is certain and cannot be refuted. They differ over the word "kadhiba". Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as a verbal noun meaning denial or refusal, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir understand it as a sense of turning back or repelling. Al-Razi offers several readings of the "lying soul" phrase.

Most commentaries say little more about the detail of lowering and raising. Ibn Kathir and al-Biqa'i remind the reader that in truth God alone lowers and raises.

This passage of Surat al-Waqi'a describes the great upheaval of the Day of Resurrection, when the earth is violently shaken and the mountains are crushed into scattered dust. The commentators agree that the 'Waqi'a' is the Resurrection and that 'raj' means an intense shaking or quaking. They also agree that the mountains are pulverised until they become like moistened flour; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya favour this meaning of crushing, drawing on the Arabic usage of 'busisa'. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan also mention the sense of breaking to pieces, while al-Kalbi, Ibn Zayd and others understand 'bass' as driving or moving, so that the mountains are set in motion and uprooted, as other verses also say. On the word 'haba' munbath', opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it to be the shaft of sunlight entering through an opening, Ali ibn Abi Talib the dust raised by animals' hooves, Ibn 'Abbas in another report sparks from a fire, and Qatada dry leaves scattered by the wind. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the first view the best, whereas al-Tabari finds it weak in one of its transmissions. The commentators agree that these images express the immensity of the terror of that Day and the complete transformation of the earth's familiar order.

This verse of Surat al-Waqi'a describes the upheaval of the earth on the Day of Resurrection. The commentators explain that the earth will be shaken violently until everything built upon it collapses, and that the mountains will be crushed into pieces, like moistened flour, or uprooted and set in motion until they become scattered dust. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, as reported by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others, agree that the verb « bussat » means to be pulverised; al-Tabari quotes a line by a thief from Ghatafan about bread and bisaysa, flour or roasted barley mixed with liquid and eaten as provision. Al-Hasan al-Basri takes it to mean being torn out from the roots, al-Suddi and Ikrima mean being broken, while al-Kalbi and Muhammad ibn Ka'b understand it as being set moving, a view also held by Abu Zayd. Regarding « habaa », Ali ibn Abi Talib says it is the dust raised by the hooves of animals, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid say a ray of sunlight entering through a window, and Ibn 'Abbas in another report, like Qatada, says it is sparks from fire or dry leaves scattered by the wind. Al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention the view that it is dust raised by horses. The commentators treat this as one of the terrors of the end of time, preceding the division of mankind into three groups described later, and none of them settles the matter by preferring one explanation of the word « habaa » over another.

The commentators explain the phrase "then they became scattered dust" as describing the fate of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection, after the earth is violently shaken and the mountains are crumbled to pieces: they become fine dust scattered in every direction. All agree that hiba' is fine dust and that munbaththan means dispersed or spread out, but they differ on what this dust actually is. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as the sunlight entering through a window, which appears like floating dust. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib understands it as the dust raised by the hooves of horses and animals, which then settles, a view also reported by Ibn Qutayba and Ibn Kathir. Ibn 'Abbas, in another report, and 'Ata' understand it as the sparks thrown off by a blazing fire that become nothing once they fall. Qatada compares it to dry leaves and foliage that the wind scatters. Al-Sam'ani reports that some take it to be ashes. As for the adjective, most read it as scattered, al-Zamakhshari and al-Biqa'i as spread out, and Abu Hayyan records al-Nakha'i's reading munbattan, meaning cut off. The commentators present these views without judging between them; what they share is that the mountains end in complete dispersal, leaving nothing standing.

This verse states that on the Day of Resurrection people will be divided into three kinds, and the commentators explain that the word "pairs" (azwaj) here means kinds or categories. The following verses describe them: the companions of the right (ashab al-maymana), who are the people of Paradise, taken on the right side and given their record in their right hand; the companions of the left (ashab al-mash'ama), who are the people of the Fire, taken on the left side and given their record in their left hand; and the foremost (al-sabiqun), who hastened to faith and obedience. The commentators agree that the address is general to all people, and that the companions of the right are the people of Paradise while the companions of the left are the people of the Fire, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report. They differ on the meaning of right and left. Al-Hasan and al-Rabi' take them to mean those blessed or unfortunate through their own deeds, Ibn Jurayj to mean those with good and bad deeds, Zayd ibn Aslam refers to the right and left sides of Adam when his offspring were taken out, and Ibn Abbas to their position at Adam's right and left. As for the foremost, al-Hasan and Qatada identify them as the first to believe in every nation, Ibn Sirin as those who prayed toward both qiblas, 'Uthman ibn Abi Sawda as those who go earliest to the mosque and leave first for the struggle, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b as the prophets. Ibn Kathir considers all these views sound, since they all describe those who hasten to good deeds. Al-Zamakhshari and others explain the repetition of the word as emphasis.

This passage of al-Waqi'a divides humankind on the Day of Resurrection into three groups, and the phrase "The companions of the right hand — what companions of the right hand!" opens by exalting their condition. The commentators explain that they are those who are led to the right, toward Paradise, or who receive their record in their right hand. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report these explanations, and al-Suyuti summarizes them as people raised in honor by entering Paradise.

Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi link the expression to the moment when God brought forth the offspring from Adam's loins: those on his right are destined for Paradise. Zayd ibn Aslam takes up the idea of Adam's right side. Al-Hasan and al-Rabi' describe them as the blessed upon themselves, those who were fortunate through their deeds. Ibn Jurayj identifies them with the people of good deeds.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the vocabulary of right and left comes from Arab usage, where passage of a bird on the right was welcomed and passage on the left was feared. Ibn 'Ashur also notes that the repetition of the term serves exaltation and wonder, leaving the listener to picture the greatness of this state.

The commentators thus agree on the identity of the group, the people of Paradise, and on the force of the phrase, while their explanations of the name vary according to how each understands the right hand. God alone knows the exact intended meaning.

This verse announces that on the Day of Resurrection people will be divided into three groups. The companions of the right hand are the blessed, who will receive their records in their right hands or be led to Paradise on the right; the companions of the left are the wretched, who will receive their records in their left hands and go to the Fire. The commentators agree that the question about the companions of the right is meant to exalt their rank, and the question about the companions of the left to express the horror of their fate. The Arabs called the left hand the 'inauspicious hand', which gave the words right and left the sense of good and bad fortune. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy record several explanations: al-Suddi says the companions of the right are the majority of the people of Paradise and those of the left the majority of the people of Hell; Ibn Abbas refers to the moment when God drew Adam's descendants from his loins; and Zayd ibn Aslam speaks of the right and left sides of Adam. Al-Hasan and al-Rabi' understand them as those blessed or cursed by their own deeds. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy explain the use of the words right and left by the value attached to them. As for the foremost, opinions differ: al-Hasan and Qatada see them as those who first embraced faith in each community, Ibn Sirin as those who prayed facing both qiblas, Uthman ibn Abi Sawda as those who went earliest to the mosque, and Mujahid as those who were first to fight in God's path. Ibn Kathir considers all these views valid, since they all express eagerness for good deeds.

The verse "And the foremost, the foremost" names the third category of people on the Day of Judgment, after the companions of the right and the companions of the left: those who hastened to good deeds and acts of obedience. The commentators agree that the repetition serves to exalt and magnify them, as they are the highest in rank. Here precedence means eagerness toward good and attaining lofty degrees.

Opinions differ on who these foremost are. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Sirin, relates it to those who prayed toward both qiblas; Ibn Kathir also cites al-Hasan and Qatada, who held that they are those who first embraced faith in every nation. Mujahid and al-Dahhak took them to be those who were first to fight in jihad, Ibn Abbas those who first emigrated, and Ali those who first performed the five daily prayers. Ka'b and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi identified them with the prophets or with the people of the Qur'an. Al-Mawardi, reporting an opinion of Ibn Abbas, named four individuals, including Abu Bakr and Umar.

Al-Zamakhshari described them as sincere people who strove to please God, while al-Razi discussed the grammatical options of the construction and preferred that the second word is an emphasis. Ibn Kathir concluded that all these explanations are valid, since they all express the same eagerness for good deeds, and that whoever leads in this world leads in the next, because the reward matches the deed. They are called "the drawn near," and the commentators place them in gardens of delight.

This passage states that on the Day of Resurrection people will be divided into three groups, and that those who outstripped others in faith and obedience during their lives are the ones brought near to God, dwelling in gardens of bliss. The commentators explain that "those brought near" denotes the highest rank, that this nearness means favour and standing with God, and that the gardens of bliss are orchards of enduring delight. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Sa'di agree that the "foremost" are those who hasten to goodness and acts of obedience, and that this precedence covers faith, emigration, prayer, jihad and good works. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that, according to al-Hasan and Qatada, they are those who were first to believe in every nation, while Ibn Sirin restricts them to those who prayed towards both qiblas, Uthman ibn Abi Sawda identifies them as those first to the mosques and in the path of God, and Ka'b sees them as the people of the Qur'an. Muhammad ibn Ka'b names them as the prophets, and Ibn 'Abbas names four people, including Abu Bakr and Umar. On the repetition of the word "foremost", Sibawayh takes it as a predicate expressing exaltation, others as emphasis, and al-Razi sees in it a sign that their condition exceeds what human knowledge can grasp. Ibn Ashur holds that all these views are correct, since they describe those who hasten to good.

This part of the verse says that the people brought near to God will dwell in gardens of lasting bliss. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, agree that these gardens are Paradise itself, and that the phrase is an annexation of place to what is found in it, like the expression house of hospitality. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that these gardens are the highest ranks, above which no station exists. Al-Razi adds that the nearness these people enjoy resembles that of the king's companions who have no duties, and is a state of pure pleasure and rest. Ibn 'Ashur sees in these words the highest rank among the three groups. Al-Razi also notes that the definite article before bliss carries a specific sense. Regarding Talha's reading with the singular form, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note that it does not change the meaning. The commentators do not differ on the general meaning, only on details. Al-Samani alone relays a report from al-Naqqash describing the bricks and soil of Paradise, which the others do not repeat.

The commentators explain that the phrase "a multitude of the first generations" is a predicate of an implied subject: those who outstripped others in good deeds form a large group among the earlier nations and a small number of this community. The Arabic thulla means a company, which the exegetes take to refer to a few as well as many. On the meaning of "first" and "last", opinions differ. Al-Hasan, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kathir understand the first as the earlier nations and the last as this community, while others, whom Ibn Kathir prefers, take the first to be the early part of this community and the last its later part. Reports attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Sirin and al-Hasan suggest that all belong to this community. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the two verses do not abrogate each other and that the second refers to the companions of the right hand. As for the "woven" couches, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid say they are overlaid with gold, 'Ikrima says they are interlaced with pearls and rubies, al-Dahhak says they are arranged in rows, and others describe a weave like the links of a coat of mail. The righteous recline on them facing one another, with no one looking at another's back. The youths who wait on them, who remain ever young, are explained by Mujahid as immortal, by al-Farra' as wearing earrings, and by al-Hasan as remaining forever at the same young age; Ibn Jarir favours the first sense. The akwab are cups without handles or spouts, the abariq are ewers with handles and spouts, and the ka's is a cup of flowing wine. The commentators state that this wine causes neither headache nor drunkenness, and they report from Ibn 'Abbas that wine in this world has four effects, intoxication, headache, vomiting and urination, from all of which the wine of Paradise is free.

This verse describes the category of the foremost (al-sabiqun) among the people of Paradise, a great multitude of the first and a few of the last. The commentators differ on who the two groups are. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the first are the earlier nations and the last this community, but Ibn Kathir also cites al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin, who held that both groups belong to this community, and he prefers this view. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi offer other readings, and many cite the hadith that this community will make up half of the people of Paradise. Regarding the 'woven couches' (sururun mawdunatun), Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say they are interlaced with gold, Ikrima says they are latticed with pearls and rubies, and al-Dahhak says they are set in rows. The exegetes describe the reclining and face-to-face seating. Most explain that the immortal youths remain at the age of youth, while al-Farra' says they wear earrings. The commentators agree that the wine of Paradise causes neither headache nor loss of reason, and that fruit and meat are chosen as one desires. The maidens are compared to pearls kept in their shell. This bliss is a recompense for deeds, and nothing vain or sinful is heard there, only greetings of peace.

This verse describes the blessed state of the foremost, the Muqarrabun, who recline on couches. The commentators agree that the word "mawduna" means closely woven or interlaced, like the links of a coat of mail. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain that the couches are interwoven or braided with gold, and Ikrima adds that they are set with pearls and rubies. Al-Tabari also reports from al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Abbas that the couches are arranged in rows, and he cites the verse of al-A'sha and the meaning of the camel's girth strap. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi confirm that the core meaning is tight weaving. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi add that the reclining is face to face, so no one sees the back of another. Some hold that the attending youths remain forever youthful, as al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir explain, while al-Farra' gives the meaning of ear-rings, a view that al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy find less convincing. The commentators also distinguish the cups without handles from the ewers with handles and spouts, and they agree that the wine causes neither headache nor loss of reason. Ibn Kathir relates traditions about the fruit and the bird meat, though he notes that several of these reports are weak. The overall picture is of supreme comfort, companionship and beauty in Paradise.

This verse describes the condition of the foremost, those brought near to God, in the Gardens of Bliss: they recline on couches, facing one another. The commentators explain that the word mawdunah means woven or interlaced couches, like the links of a coat of mail. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that these couches are adorned with gold, pearls and jewels, following Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrimah, while al-Dahhak and another report from Ibn Abbas understand them as arranged in rows. Al-Sam'ani explains reclining as leaning for comfort. Facing one another, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain, means that no one sees the back of his companion. Al-Razi adds that no one turns his back on another, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy see in it good companionship and refined manners. The commentators agree that this honour belongs to the foremost, but differ on who the first and last are: Ibn Kathir and al-Hasan take both groups to be from this community, while al-Tabari takes the first to be earlier nations. No commentator draws a legal ruling from this verse, which only describes the splendour of the reward.

This verse describes the service given to the foremost believers in Paradise: youths circle around them with cups, ewers and a flowing cup of wine. The plain meaning, on which the commentators agree, is that these are servants who never age or change. Mujahid says they do not die, al-Hasan and al-Kalbi that they do not grow old or change, and al-Farra' notes that the Arabs call a man who grew up without greying 'mukhallad'. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi describe them as servant boys who keep the look of youth. Another reading, given by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrima and others, takes the word to mean that they wear earrings or bracelets, and al-Tabari judges that the first meaning is the more evident. As to who these youths are, Ali and al-Hasan report that they are the children of this world who had neither good nor bad deeds, while other exegetes cite a hadith about the children of unbelievers, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim stress that most hold they remain at one age. The commentators agree that the cups have no handles or spouts, that the ewers have them, and that the wine of Paradise causes neither headache nor loss of reason, unlike the wine of this world. They differ on the reading of 'yunzafun': some take it to mean that their minds are not lost, others that the drink never runs out.

This verse describes the service given to the foremost people of Paradise, who are brought cups without handles and ewers with handles and spouts, along with a cup of flowing drink. The commentators largely agree on the vocabulary. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the akwab are vessels without handles or spouts, while the abariq have them, and Ibn Juzayy adds that the ewer is what has a handle or spout. Regarding the kas, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi take it to mean wine, whereas Abu 'Ubayda defines it as the vessel together with what it holds, and al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that a vessel is called a cup only when it is full. Most scholars, including Ibn 'Abbas, take the word mu'in to mean a flowing drink, and al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya add that it is not pressed out as wine is in this world. There is consensus that this drink causes neither headache nor loss of reason, unlike worldly wine. On the meaning of yusadda'un, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it as headache, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi also cite the sense of not scattering. On yunzafun, al-Tabari reports the majority reading as meaning not losing one's mind, and the Kufan reading as meaning that the drink never runs out. Finally, several commentators, including Ibn Kathir, note that the verse shows reward matching deeds.

This verse describes the drink served to the foremost, those brought near to God, in the Garden: a cup of flowing wine that causes neither headache nor loss of reason, unlike the wine of this world. The commentators agree on this general meaning. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Abbas and al-Razi explain that they will not suffer headache from it, while others, including al-Tabari in citing a reading of Mujahid, read it as they will not be scattered from it or their pleasure will not be cut off. As for the word yunzafun, the majority take it to mean that their reason will not be taken away by drunkenness, while the Kufan readers, who read it with a kasra, understand that their wine will not run out. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi note that both readings are known. The following verses also mention fruits of their choosing, the flesh of birds, large-eyed houris, and speech free of vanity and sin, only words of peace, according to al-Qurtubi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir.

This verse describes what the foremost, those brought near, will receive in Paradise: fruits they choose from among many kinds, and the flesh of birds as they desire. The commentators explain that choosing means taking the best and what pleases them, and that desire refers to what the souls long for. Most exegetes connect the word "fruit" to what precedes it, namely the cups and jugs carried around by the young servants. Al-Alusi, who addresses the difficulty, answers that this service takes place during drinking and is a mark of honour to the guests, and notes that fruit may be served before meat because it is lighter on the stomach. Al-Razi explains that fruit is always present and one chooses among it, while meat is desired when appetite arises. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate reports about a bird that alights before the believer, roasted or fried as he wishes, though Ibn Kathir acknowledges the weakness of several chains. Some readers take the words in the accusative or nominative without changing the general sense. Abu Hayyan judges too remote the idea that the genitive depends on the gardens. The shared view is that this bounty is both material and spiritual, drawing on the best that people know, and stressing the completeness of choice and contentment.

These verses describe the blessings of the foremost, those brought near to God, in Paradise: they recline on couches woven and set with gold and precious stones, facing one another, with no one looking at another's back. Youths who remain forever young attend them. They are served cups, pitchers and a cup of flowing wine, a wine that neither gives headaches nor takes away reason, unlike the wine of this world. They are offered whatever fruit they choose and the flesh of birds as they desire, and there are wide-eyed houris, pure as hidden pearls. The commentators explain that all this is a reward for their deeds, and that the people of Paradise hear there no vain talk or sinful speech, only words of peace. The commentators agree that the foremost are a multitude of earlier nations and a few of this community, but they differ on the meaning of 'the earlier' and 'the later': al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir take them to be the early and later generations of this community, while al-Tabari takes the earlier to mean the past nations. They also differ on the 'everlasting youths': Mujahid and Ibn Abbas say they do not die or change, Sa'id ibn Jubayr says they wear earrings, and Ali and al-Hasan say they are the children of the people of this world. On the word 'yunzafun', some read it with a fatha meaning their minds are not taken away, others with a kasra meaning their drink does not run out, and al-Tabari considers both readings valid. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain why fruit is mentioned before meat, and Ibn al-Qayyim reports the views on whether birds' flesh in Paradise is cooked.

This verse describes the wide-eyed maidens, the houris, whom God has prepared for the foremost believers in Paradise. The commentators explain that hur means women with very white skin and very dark pupils, and ʿin means those with large, beautiful eyes. The readings differ on the case of wa-ḥūrun. Most read it in the nominative, either as a continuation of the servants or as an implied 'for them.' Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read it in the genitive, matching the preceding nouns, meaning 'and with houris,' a common Arabic device that al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari illustrate with poetry. Qutrub allows that they may be brought round to the believers as a pleasure. Some read the accusative, implying 'and they will be given.' As for the comparison with the hidden pearl, al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the brilliant purity of their complexion and beauty, citing a hadith from Umm Salama comparing it to a pearl in its shell. Al-Razi adds that 'maknun' means a pearl untouched by sun and air. Mujahid says they are called houris because the gaze is dazzled by them. Al-Tabari also reports views that they were created from saffron, which the other commentators do not endorse. All stress that this bounty is the reward for good deeds, and that the people of Paradise hear no idle talk or sin there, only the word of peace, which Ibn 'Abbas and others understand as greetings among them and from the angels.

This verse describes part of the delights of the people of Paradise: the wide-eyed houris, whose whiteness and beauty are compared to pearls kept hidden in their shells. The commentators broadly agree on this meaning. They also agree that the pearl is called hidden because it is guarded from hands, dust and sunlight, which keeps it pure and bright. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi relate reports about the beauty of these women, including the hadith from Umm Salama comparing their purity to a pearl in its shell, which Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy also cite. Readers differ over the case of the word hur. Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj explain the genitive reading as agreement with the preceding words, since the houris are not literally served like drinks or fruit, and al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash also justify it by meaning. Others, such as Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, prefer the nominative, meaning that there are houris for them. Al-Tabari judges that both readings are correct and close in meaning. As for the sense of hur, Ibn Abbas understands it as blackness of the pupil, al-Hasan as virtuous women, and Mujahid as eyes that are dazzled. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi stress the comparison with the pearl. Al-Zamakhshari links the closing phrase, a reward for what they did, to the completion of their bliss: they hear neither idle talk nor sin, only the words of peace, understood as mutual greetings or the greeting of the angels.

This part of the verse explains that all the blessings just described, including the wide-eyed houris likened to pearls kept safe in their shells, the ever-youthful attendants, the cups, and the fruit and bird meat, are a reward given to the foremost believers for the good deeds they did in this world. Al-Tabari and others explain that the word jaza' is either an object of purpose or a verbal noun, and that it means a recompense from God for obedience. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin hold that the preposition bi indicates cause rather than exact exchange, since no one's deeds can match the value of God's favour, and they cite the hadith that no one enters Paradise by his works alone. They add that entry itself comes from God's mercy, while ranks and dwellings are distributed according to deeds, a view also reported by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi contrast this with the punishment of the disbelievers, which they describe as no more than the measure of what they did. Thus the reward is not strictly proportional wages but a grace that honours those who acted well.

This verse says that the people of Paradise will hear there no idle talk and no speech that would make them sinful, only a word free of every flaw: the greeting of peace. The commentators agree that the verse removes from Paradise every vain or hurtful word and affirms that its people greet one another. Ibn 'Abbas took 'laghw' to mean false speech, Mujahid took it to mean insults, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b took 'ta'thim' to mean that they do not accuse one another of sin; Ibn Juzayy adds that the sin lies in blaming another. On the exception 'except a word', most treat it as a disconnected exception, meaning 'but they hear a good word', while al-Razi allows it to be read as connected, as a rhetorical emphasis in denying idle talk. Grammarians differ on 'salaman salaman': al-Zajjaj took it as a verbal noun governed by 'speech', others as an apposition or a qualifier of 'qawl'. Ibn Kathir holds that they greet one another, and Ibn al-Qayyim notes that the negation implies the affirmation of its opposite, peace. Al-Razi sees the repetition as a sign of complete blessing, since worldly greeting is complete only when answered.

This verse describes the bliss of the people of Paradise. The commentators explain that they hear there neither vain talk nor any words that would cause sin, but only a word free of defects, namely the greeting they exchange. Al-Tabari notes that (salaman salaman) may be read as an apposition to (qilan), the greeting being the speech itself, or as a direct object of (qilan) meaning 'except a word of peace'. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider the exception to be disjunctive, since the greeting does not belong to the category of idle talk. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Zajjaj explain that the sense is that they greet one another, one greeting after another. Al-Razi observes that the repetition of the greeting marks the completion of the blessing. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di see in it the fine manners of the people of Paradise in their speech. Ibn Abbas states that they greet each other, and al-Baghawi reports that the angels also greet them.

This verse introduces the people of the right hand, those given their record in their right hand. They rank below the foremost who are brought near, yet the Qur'an extols them with the phrase "what are the people of the right hand!" The commentators describe their blessings: lote trees without thorns or heavy with fruit, talh trees arranged in tiers, a lasting shade that the sun does not dispel, water flowing constantly, abundant fruit neither cut off nor forbidden, and raised couches. On the thornless lote, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Qatada and Ibn Kaysan say its thorns were removed, while Mujahid and al-Dahhak take it to mean laden with fruit; Ibn al-Qayyim considers both views compatible, since God removed the thorns and put fruit in their place. As for the talh, Ibn Abbas, Ali, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, Ata and Mujahid identify it as the banana tree, though al-Hasan says it is a tree with cool shade, and al-Farra' and Abu Ubayda describe a large thorny tree. Ali is reported to have read "talʿ" (fruit clusters) instead, a reading not adopted in the codex. Several commentators link the extended shade to a tree in Paradise under which a rider travels for a hundred years, while others understand it as permanent shade. The raised couches are taken by some as cushions and by others as a reference to the wives. The houris are created anew, made virgins, loving to their husbands and of the same age. Finally, the commentators differ on the two groups: some say they are from earlier nations and from this community, others say both belong to the community of Muhammad.

This verse describes the blessings of the people of the right, the believers and doers of good whose record is given into their right hands. God says they will be among lote trees without thorns, sidr makhdud. The commentators agree on the general sense that these blessings are presented in images familiar to desert dwellers. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Qatada and others take makhdud to mean thornless, while Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Muqatil take it to mean laden with fruit. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim reconcile both readings by saying God removed the thorns and replaced them with abundant fruit. For talh, most exegetes, including Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and Ibn Zayd, identify it as the banana tree, al-Hasan says it is a tree with cool shade and not a banana, and al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda describe a large thorny tree known to the Arabs. A reading talh with an 'ayn is attributed to 'Ali, which Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir mention with caution. The extended shade is understood as lasting and without sun, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of the tree whose shade a rider cannot cross in a hundred years. The water flows without channels, and the fruit is never cut off or forbidden. The raised couches are interpreted by some as beds and by others as the wives, whether the houris or women of this world.

This verse describes the bliss of the companions of the right in Paradise, the righteous believers who rank below the foremost. The commentators explain that the lote tree without thorns (sidr makhdud) is one whose thorns have been cut away, as Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and others say, while Mujahid takes it to mean a tree heavy with fruit, and several scholars consider both meanings to be intended. The banana tree is the view of most exegetes, including Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, al-Hasan, Ikrima, Qatada and Mujahid; Ali is reported to have read it as talh with a ayn and to have refused to change the Mushaf. Al-Hasan says it is a tree with cool shade, while al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda describe a large thorny tree known to the Arabs, and al-Zajjaj identifies it with umm Ghaylan. Mandud means tiered from base to top with fruit. The extended shade is one that never recedes, and many link it to the hadith of a tree under which a rider travels for a hundred years. Flowing water (ma' maskub) runs without a channel, and the abundant fruit is neither cut off nor forbidden. The raised couches are understood by most as high beds, and by some as a reference to the wives. The commentators note that these details are offered to people of the desert, who admired water, shade and trees.

This verse describes part of the bliss of the people of the right in Paradise: an extended shade, meaning one that is lasting and does not pass away under the sun. The commentators explain that Paradise is entirely shaded, with no sun, and that its shade stretches out and spreads without contracting. They agree that this shade is permanent, and they refer to the hadith reported by Abu Hurayra and others, in which a rider could travel for a hundred years in the shade of a tree of Paradise without crossing it; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi cite this hadith. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi understand the shade to be that of the trees, whereas al-Qurtubi also reports, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, that it is the shade of the Throne. Amr ibn Maymun speaks of a distance of seventy thousand years, or five hundred thousand years in another transmission. Al-Razi offers several meanings: an unending duration, a spatial extent, or a shade created by God rather than the shade of trees. Abu 'Ubayda and others note that the Arabs call whatever does not end 'extended', and they quote a line of Labid. The commentators do not settle the exact nature of this shade; they report their views and evidence as they stand, relying largely on the authentic prophetic hadith about the tree.

This verse describes the water enjoyed by the people of the right in Paradise as flowing water, poured out continuously, needing no drawing or carrying, and the commentators add that it flows without a channel. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi agree on this sense, and recall that the Arabs, living in hot and arid lands, regarded running water as a rare blessing, so the description promises comfort without toil. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand that it flows wherever and however one wishes, without effort. Al-Razi adds that it may pour from above, and sees in the phrase a way of expressing abundance, since the Arabs spoke of pouring out water as a sign of plenty. Al-Hasan al-Basri takes it to mean water that never stops flowing. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the word denotes a forceful outflow, like the rivers of Paradise. The commentators do not differ on the general meaning, only on how the image should be pictured. This water completes the scene of the shaded and flowering garden that the people of the desert could long for.

The commentators place this verse within their description of the blessings of the people of the right, whose food is an abundance of fruit. The general meaning is that they have plentiful fruit, varied in kinds and types, which never ceases at any time, unlike the fruits of this world that disappear in certain seasons, and which no thorn, distance, or price prevents anyone from reaching if he wishes. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, al-Qasimi and others agree on this general sense, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya report, citing prophetic traditions, that a fruit once picked is replaced by a similar or better one. On the negation of cutting off and prohibition, the views differ. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada explain it as not cut off by the seasons nor withheld for a price, whereas Ibn Abbas adds that it does not end once plucked and is not denied to anyone who wants it, and al-Mawardi takes it to mean that it does not perish or spoil. Al-Razi argues that denying interruption also implies denying prohibition, since worldly fruit is withheld in exchange for payment, which God does not need. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the double negation serves to exclude the opposite of what is desired. Some modern commentators, including Sayyid Qutb, observe that the verse deliberately leaves the kinds of fruit unspecified, which suited an audience of desert dwellers deprived of such produce.

This verse describes the fruit of Paradise for the companions of the right: it is not cut off by season as the fruit of this world is cut off in winter, nor is it kept away by thorns or distance, nor is it restricted by price. The commentators agree on this basic meaning. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, says that neither thorn nor distance prevents one from taking it, and that when a person desires a fruit it comes close to his hand. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that it is not cut off at any time and not withheld by payment, while al-Mawardi adds that it does not perish or spoil. Al-Razi argues that the negation of being cut off indicates lasting existence, and the negation of being prevented indicates free access.

The commentators differ on the raised couches. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take them as high-raised beds or cushions, while Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba read the word as a figure for the women of Paradise. A report from Abu Sa'id on a height of five hundred years is cited by several scholars, but al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Kathir regard its chain as weak, and Ibn al-Jawzi understands it as a matter of elevated rank.

Other points also differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report the Prophet's saying that a rider can travel for a hundred years in the shade of one tree of Paradise, which Ibn Kathir accepts as authentic. On the word 'urub, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain it as women who are loving and devoted to their husbands, some adding sweetness of speech. The scholars agree that the atrab are of the same age.

The overall meaning is a lasting abundance, offered without hindrance, which each commentator explains through his own concerns.

This verse describes the reward of the people of the right, those who will be taken to Paradise, and mentions raised couches. The commentators agree on the idea of elevation and luxury, but differ on what exactly these couches are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Samani report that they are high and soft, sometimes piled one upon another. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that their height is the distance between heaven and earth, though al-Tirmidhi himself judged it weak. Al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy understand them as literal beds or couches, and al-Razi offers three readings: high in value, stacked on top of one another, or raised above the bed frame.

A second reading, transmitted from Abu 'Ubayda and adopted by al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi, takes the word "furush" as a figure for the wives, since Arabs call a woman a bed. Al-Qasimi accepts this as possible while the verse's parallel in Surah Ya-Sin, where they recline on couches, supports the literal sense. Ibn Juzayy calls the wives reading remote. Ibn al-Qayyim cites several narrations about the distance, without settling their authenticity.

The commentators therefore retain the sense of nobility and comfort, and most reject any comparison with the beds of this world.

This verse describes the women of Paradise who are prepared for the companions of the right. God says that He created them in a new creation, distinct from their earthly existence, and made them virgins, loving toward their husbands and of equal age. The commentators agree on the general sense of beauty, purity and conjugal affection. They differ, however, on who these women are. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Muqatil and al-Zajjaj, followed by Ibn Kathir in one of his readings, understand them to be the houris, created without birth. Al-Tabari, al-Dahhak and others report that they are the women of this world, whom God renews after old age as young virgins, citing reports traced to the Prophet through Anas and Umm Salama, some of which al-Tirmidhi and others judged weak. The pronoun may also refer to the raised couches, understood as a metaphor for the wives, a view upheld by Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi, who sees in it an allusion to their rank. On the word ʿuruban, Ibn Abbas and most exegetes take it to mean women who are loving and devoted to their husbands. Ikrima reads it as coquettish, and Zayd ibn Aslam as eloquent in speech. On atrab, most read it as women of the same age, which some fix at thirty-three years. Al-Razi adds that virginity in Paradise differs from virginity in this world.

The commentators explain that God's words "We made them virgins" mean that He makes the women of Paradise virgins, untouched before their husbands, and that this virginity endures, so that each time a husband comes to them he finds them virgins. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report mainly the view that these are the women of this world who, having become old, are re-created young and virgin, as narrations attributed to Umm Salama and Anas ibn Malik indicate, though some of their transmitters are judged weak. Others, such as Ibn Abbas as cited by al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, speak of the houris created afresh, and Ibn Abbas adds that no husband comes to them without finding them virgins. Al-Razi argues that if the phrase meant an initial creation, virginity would need no stating, so he takes it as a re-creation, while noting other readings. As for "'urub", al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi take it to mean women who are loving and winsome toward their husbands, while others understand eloquent women or those who are good wives; the word is glossed differently across dialects, with "shakila" in Mecca and "ghanija" in Medina. "Atrab" means women of the same age, which some fix at thirty-three, others at the same character or the same appearance. The commentators thus agree on the beauty and tenderness of these wives, but differ on the nature of their creation and the precise meaning of the descriptive terms.

This verse describes the companions of the right hand's spouses in Paradise. The commentators explain that God created them anew, made them virgins, 'urub (loving and devoted to their husbands) and atrab (of the same age). There is wide agreement on the meaning of 'urub: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr describe women ardently in love with their husbands, Ikrima says they are coquettish, Tamim ibn Hadhlam says they are good in marital intimacy, and Zayd ibn Aslam says they have eloquent speech. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi cite the hadith of Umm Salama that these are the elderly women of this world, restored as young virgins after old age, while al-Biqa'i reports Ibn Hajar judging its chains weak. On atrab, most take it to mean equal in age, thirty-three years according to Ibn Kathir, whereas al-Sudd i understands agreement of character. Al-Razi considers whether the pronoun refers to the houris or to the women of this world. The reading 'urban with a silent vowel is attributed to Tamim and Bakr, and al-Tabari considers the reading with damma more correct.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the companions of the right, the believers who will be led to Paradise on the right side. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, God will create for them wives in a new and perfect form: virgins, loving toward their husbands, and of the same age. The scholars differ on who these wives are. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and others take them to be the women of this world who were old and are recreated young, relying on reports from Umm Salama and Anas ibn Malik. Al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari hold that they are the houris created from the start, al-Razi allows both readings, and Ibn Ashur considers that the re-creation covers both groups. On the word 'urub, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada explain it as women who are affectionate and devoted to their husbands, Ikrima as coquettish, and Zayd ibn Aslam as eloquent in speech. The word atrab means, according to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, of the same age; al-Sudi understands it as harmony of character, with no hatred or envy among them. The commentators also note that the phrase for the companions of the right may attach either to the creation or to the word of equal age. Finally, the phrase a troop from the earlier and a troop from the later generations refers for most to the earlier nations and the community of Muhammad, but Abu al-'Aliya, Mujahid, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak hold that both troops belong to this community, a view that a report from Ibn Abbas appears to support. These discussions mainly aim to convey the greatness of the reward granted to these believers.

This verse describes the companions of the right, the righteous who are not among the foremost brought near: they are a great multitude of the earlier peoples and a great multitude of the later ones. The commentators differ on who these two groups are. Al-Tabari reports from al-Hasan and Mujahid that the first group refers to the earlier nations and the second to the community of Muhammad, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi report that, for al-Hasan and others, the earlier ones are the former peoples and the later ones this community. Others, cited by Abu al-Su'ud, al-Shawkani and Ibn Kathir, hold that both groups belong entirely to this community, relying on a report from Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Bakra. Abu Hayyan and Ibn al-Qayyim add the reports on the proportion of the saved within the Muslim community.

The commentators agree on the description of this reward: the thornless lote tree, the banana tree with its layered fruit, the extended shade, flowing water, abundant fruit never cut off or forbidden, and raised couches. They differ on the meaning of the terms. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid explain the lote as the thornless jujube, while Mujahid sees a tree heavy with fruit; al-Hasan denies that the talh is the banana. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur stress that this rank comes below the foremost. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir relate reports about the spouses, and the word 'urub is understood by some as women who love their husbands and by others as graceful or well-spoken.

The overall message is clear: the verse exalts the reward of the companions of the right, while the details and the identity of the two groups remain matters the scholars discuss.

This verse says that the people of the right hand, meaning the righteous who believed and did good, are a great company among the earlier nations and a great company among the later believers of this community. The commentators broadly agree that the 'earlier' refers to past nations or the first generations of this community, and the 'later' to the community of Muhammad or its final generations. Al-Tabari and al-Hasan take the earlier to be past nations and the later to be the community of Muhammad, while Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliya, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak explain that the earlier are the foremost of this community and the later its late members. A hadith related through Ibn 'Abbas says both groups belong entirely to the Prophet's community, and al-Tha'alibi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi transmit both opinions. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings of 'people of the right', including Maymun ibn Mihran's view that they rank below the close ones, and al-Hasan's view that they are the good followers. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim cite the hadith of the hundred and twenty rows of Paradise, eighty of them from this community, and the Prophet's words about a quarter, a third and a half. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the difference from verse 14 lies in the distinction between the foremost and the people of the right. Ibn 'Ashur observes that placing this group after the description of their reward signals that they are less rare than the foremost. Several reports from the time of revelation say that 'Umar wept when told that the saved would be few, and that this verse was revealed to comfort him.

This verse describes the people of the left, those who will be taken by the left side to the Fire, and the commentators read the repeated question as an expression of the enormity of their state. They agree that their punishment includes a scorching wind that penetrates the pores, boiling water, and a shade of black smoke that is neither cool nor pleasant. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most others take the blackness to be smoke, while Ibn Abbas in another report says it is the enclosure of the Fire surrounding its people, Ibn Kaysan holds that it is one of the names of Hell, and Ibn Zayd and Ibn Buraida describe it as a black mountain in the Fire. On the phrase neither cool nor generous, Qatada explains that the place of rest is not cool and the sight is not pleasant, al-Dahhak says it is not sweet, al-Farra and Ibn al-Jawzi note the Arabic habit of attaching the word generous to any negated quality meant as blame, and al-Zamakhshari reads it as mockery. The commentators link their fate to their luxury in worldly life and their persistence in the great sin, which al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take to be polytheism, while al-Sha'bi takes it to be the false oath. The verse also records their denial of resurrection, which they found hard to believe after they had become dust and bones. God answers that the first and the last will be gathered at an appointed time, after which they will eat from the zaqqum tree and drink like thirsty camels, and this will be their welcome on the Day of Judgement.

This verse describes the fate of the people of the left, those who will be taken to the fire on the left side. The commentators agree that they will be in samum, a scorching wind that penetrates the pores, and in hamim, water heated to its utmost. As for the shade of yahmum, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, understand it to be a jet-black smoke. Ibn Abbas also reports that it is the enclosing wall of fire around its people, Ibn Kaysan takes it as one of the names of Hell, and Ibn Buraydah and Ibn Zayd describe a black mountain of fire to which the damned flee in vain.

The phrase neither cool nor generous is read by many as irony: this shade has neither the coolness nor the benefit of ordinary shade. Qatada explains that it has neither a cool place nor a pleasing view, and Dahhak takes generous to mean sweet, not bitter. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note that denying a praiseworthy quality in this way affirms its opposite.

The commentators explain that these people had been pampered and absorbed in pleasures in worldly life, and that they persisted in the great oath or the great sin. For al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd this is associating partners with God; for Qatada and Mujahid, it is the grave sin they would not repent of; for al-Sha'bi, it is the false oath.

This verse describes what awaits the companions of the left, those who associated others with God and persisted in sin. They will be in a scorching wind that penetrates the pores, in boiling water, and in a shade of smoke. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, agree that the shade is thick black smoke, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid in particular, and that the Arabs call anything intensely black yahmum. Ibn Abbas also gives another view, that it is the enclosure of fire surrounding its people, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy mention that it is a mountain in Hell according to Ibn Buraydah and Ibn Zayd. Saying the shade is neither cool nor pleasant negates the usual qualities of shade. Al-Tabari and al-Farra' explain that the word karim is only a particle the Arabs add after a negation, without a separate meaning, while Qatada speaks of a place neither cool nor pleasant to look at, and al-Dahhak of water that is not sweet. Several scholars, including Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi, see this as mockery toward the damned. The verse then gives the reason, namely their worldly luxury and their persistence in the great sin. Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd identify it as shirk, Qatada and Mujahid as a grave sin they never repented of, and al-Sha'bi as the false oath. Many commentators link this stubbornness to their denial of resurrection.

This verse describes the people of the left, those who will be taken to the Fire by the left side. The commentators explain that they will be in a scorching wind that penetrates the pores, in water heated to the utmost, and under a shade of intensely black smoke. On the nature of this shade, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Malik, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and most exegetes take it to be smoke, while Ibn 'Abbas also describes it as the enclosure of fire that surrounds the damned, and others such as Ibn Buraydah and Ibn Zayd describe it as a mountain in Hell to which the damned flee for shelter, or, according to Ibn Kaysan, a name of Hell.

As for the phrase 'neither cool nor pleasant', all agree that it denies this shade the coolness and benefit that a shade normally gives, since it is hot and harmful. Qatada explains: neither cool in its dwelling nor pleasant to look at; al-Dahhak understands it as not sweet to drink; Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab as not pleasing in appearance. Al-Tabari and al-Farra' note that the Arabs attach the word 'generous' to whatever quality they deny, to express blame, and al-Mawardi adds that there is no honour for those who sit in it.

The commentators link this punishment to the conduct of the damned: they lived in luxury, according to Ibn 'Abbas, or in polytheism, according to al-Suddi, and they persisted in the great oath-breaking, which for most means associating partners with God, as al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd say. Qatada and Mujahid take it to be the great sin they did not repent of, and al-Sha'bi the false oath. Several connect it with the denial of resurrection.

This passage describes the People of the Left, the inhabitants of the Fire, and explains why they suffer. The commentators say they will be exposed to a scorching wind that penetrates the pores, to boiling water, and to a shade of intensely black smoke, which is neither cool nor pleasant nor honourable. Most exegetes identify the shade as smoke: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Malik and Ibn Zayd say so, while al-Mawardi reports from Ibn Abbas that it is a black fire, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi stress its extreme blackness. As for the denial of coolness and generosity, Qatada explains it as a place that is neither cool nor pleasant to look at, al-Dahhak as a lack of sweetness, and al-Mawardi and al-Razi as a total absence of honour for those who shelter there. The reason given for their punishment is that in worldly life they were affluent and absorbed in pleasures, which kept them from reflection and obedience. On the phrase 'persisting in the great violation', al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd understand it as polytheism or a great sin they never repent of, al-Sha'bi understands it as the false oath, and al-Razi and Ibn Ashur note that it includes denying the resurrection. The passage ends with their denial of resurrection and God's reply that the first and last generations will be gathered at an appointed time.

This part of the verse describes the people of the left, the disbelievers who are led by the left side to the Fire. They suffer a scorching wind, boiling water and a shade of intensely black smoke that is neither cool nor pleasant. The commentators explain that the reason is that they lived in luxury and self-indulgence (mutrafun), heedless of reflection, and persisted in a great sin without repenting. The scholars differ on what this sin was. Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir understand it as shirk, associating others with God. Qatada and Mujahid take it as the grave sin they would not repent of, while al-Sha'bi holds that it is the false oath (al-yamin al-ghamus). Some connect the verse with denying the resurrection and with the oaths sworn to that effect. Ibn Zayd explains that persisting (yusirrun) means remaining on the sin without giving it up. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the word "luxury" is not a condemnation of comfort in itself, but shows how it led to arrogance and neglect of the truth. As for the shade, Ibn Abbas and others say it is smoke, Ibn Abbas adding that it is the enclosure of the Fire, and Ibn Zayd that it is a mountain in Hell. The phrase "neither cool nor generous" negates the two usual qualities of shade: it gives no relief and honours no one who seeks it. The exegetes agree that this fate follows from persistence in error and forgetfulness of God's favours.

This verse reports the words of those who denied resurrection: they wondered whether, once they had died and become dust and bones, they could be raised again, and asked the same about their forefathers. The commentators read the questions as expressions of denial, mockery and rejection of the resurrection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy report that they persisted in their error, and they differ on the phrase the great perjury or sin (al-hinth al-'azim). Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd take it to mean associating partners with God, Qatada and Mujahid take it as the great sin they never repented of, and al-Sha'bi takes it as the false oath. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that they also swore that there would be no resurrection, and Ibn 'Atiyya judges shirk the most apparent meaning. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi add that this stance went with idolatry and pride. Readers differ on the two interrogative particles: Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far keep only one interrogative. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the mention of a time serves to strengthen the denial of resurrection in general, not to limit it to that state. Al-Razi links the luxury mentioned in the surrounding verses to heedlessness, which turns people away from reflection. God's answer follows in the next verses: all the first and last generations will be gathered at an appointed day, the Day of Resurrection.

This verse records the denial of the disbelievers, who found resurrection impossible once they had become dust and bones, and asked whether their earliest forefathers would also be raised. Al-Tabari and those who followed him read the question as a rejection and a mockery, understanding by the earliest ones the ancestors who had passed away. The commentators agree that the divine answer that follows dismisses this objection by announcing that the earliest and the latest will be gathered for an appointed known day, which is the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur report that this denial was their constant habit. The great persistence they held to is, according to most, polytheism, as Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid say. Al-Sha'bi identifies it as the false oath, and a report from Qatada also presents it as a grave sin they never repented of. Al-Alusi quotes al-Subki, who reads it as the oath denying resurrection, a reading he finds consistent with what follows. Al-Razi stresses the sense of denial and the strength of the emphatic forms used. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the conjunction placed after the interrogative particle requires a grammatical explanation, on which the commentators agree. As for the readings, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read the particle 'aw with a sukun on the waw, while the majority read it with a vowel.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to answer those who deny the resurrection: the first and the last of mankind will all be gathered at an appointed day, which is the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand "the first" as the forefathers and earlier nations, and "the last" as the people who come after them. Al-Razi explains that mentioning the first before the last answers their doubt about their ancestors more forcefully, and that the word "gathered" is stronger than mere resurrection because it refers to being brought to the place of reckoning. Ibn Kathir states that the gathering includes everyone, neither earlier nor later than the set time. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the emphatic particles strengthen the announcement. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that this day is known to God alone. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the "miqat" is the fixed term appointed for the world. The commentators agree on the general meaning, while their wording differs on who the first and last are and on the force of the emphasis. The verse prepares the description of the fate of the deniers that follows.

The commentators explain that this verse answers the disbelievers' denial of resurrection, when they ask whether they will be raised once they have become dust and bones. God tells His Prophet to say that the first and the last of mankind, their forefathers and their descendants, will all be gathered at an appointed, known time, which is the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and others keep to this plain sense. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the construction 'mīqāt yawm' uses the sense of 'from', and that the mīqāt is the fixed limit, like the boundaries for entering Mecca in pilgrimage. Al-Razi sees in the word 'say' and in placing the earlier generations first a rhetorical reply to their doubt about their ancestors, and in the emphatic 'lamajmū'ūn' a gathering on the field of judgment that goes beyond mere resurrection. Ibn 'Ashur adds that all will be raised on one single day, not in successive waves as death came. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that only God knows that day. The verses that follow describe, in an ironic tone, the food and drink of the misguided, and Ibn Kathir and others point out that this is their 'nuzul', the welcome given to a guest.

This verse addresses those who went astray and denied the Resurrection. The commentators explain that after they are gathered for judgment, they will eat from the tree of zaqqum, a bitter and repulsive tree, filling their bellies with it out of intense hunger. They will then drink on top of it boiling water, the hamim, and they will drink as thirsty camels drink, the hiym, which are never satisfied. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the address to refer to the Quraysh and those in their condition, while al-Razi and Abu Hayyan read it as a general address to every straying denier. All agree that dalal means straying from guidance and takdhib means rejecting the Resurrection, the promise and the threat. On the word hiym, Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars take it to mean thirsty camels afflicted with the disease of hayam, whereas al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Uyayna take it to be sandy ground that never absorbs water. On recitation, Nafi', 'Asim and Hamza read shurb with a damma, while the rest read it with a fatha; both are accepted as valid dialects. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the second drinking heightens the wonder at their condition, since they drink eagerly what burns them. Finally, this food and drink is their nuzul on the Day of Judgment, a word normally meaning the welcome given to a guest, used here ironically as in the verse announcing a painful punishment.

This verse describes the fate of those who went astray and denied the Resurrection: on the Day of Judgment they will eat from the tree of zaqqum, a bitter tree repugnant in both sight and taste, and they will fill their bellies with it because of intense hunger. They will then drink boiling water on top of it, drinking like thirsty camels, the hīm. The commentators regard this food and drink as their nuzul, their welcome, and many read it as mockery, as in the verse announcing a painful punishment. All agree that the address is directed at the Quraysh and those like them, that straying means turning away from guidance, and that denial means rejecting the Resurrection and the divine threat. They differ on the nature of the zaqqum: al-Baydawi and al-Razi describe a small tree with foul, bitter leaves growing in Tihama, while Ibn Kathir reports that it names any food hard to swallow. On the word hīm, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrima take it to mean thirsty camels, al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Uyayna mean sandy land, and al-Suddi a disease that prevents any quenching of thirst. The readings differ on the vowel of shurb between damma and fatha; al-Zamakhshari takes the fatha form as the verbal noun and the damma form as the thing drunk. The hamim is water of extreme heat, and the shade of yahmum is, for most, black smoke, while Ibn Zayd describes a mountain in hell. The commentators note that negating coolness and goodness from this shade serves to stress its harm.

This verse describes the fate of the astray deniers on the Day of Judgment: they will eat from the tree of zaqqum, a bitter, foul-tasting and ugly tree, and they will fill their bellies with it because of their extreme hunger. The commentators agree on the general meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the pronoun in "minha" refers to the tree, whose name may be treated as feminine or masculine. Al-Tabari prefers the feminine because of the meaning, and al-Zamakhshari, followed by Abu Hayyan, notes that it is feminine in meaning while the pronoun in "alayhi" is masculine in form. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi observe that filling the belly adds to the punishment, since they are not satisfied with the small quantity that a person eats in this world. The drinking that follows is of scalding water, al-hamim, which they drink like thirsty camels.
