On the word al-hiim, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrima take it to mean thirsty camels afflicted by a disease that prevents them from being satisfied, while al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Uyayna take it to mean soft sandy ground that never takes in enough water. Readings of "shurba" differ, with Nafi', Asim and Hamza reading it with a damma and the others with a fatha, both being accepted. Finally, the word nuzul means what is prepared for a guest, and several commentators, such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi, see it as irony toward these deniers.

This passage describes the fate of the people of the left in the Fire: according to the commentators, they eat from the tree of zaqqum until their bellies are full, then drink on top of it boiling water, the hamim. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur mostly hold that the word hiym means thirsty camels afflicted with the disease of hiyam, which leaves them unable to quench their thirst, so the sense is a thirst that is never satisfied. Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima, Qatada and others agree, and al-Mawardi and al-Razi also state this view. Another reading, transmitted by al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir from al-Dahhak, Ibn 'Uyayna and Ibn Kaysan, takes it as sandy soil that soaks up water without ever filling. Al-Mawardi also reports the view of Khalid ibn Ma'dan, who describes drinking in one gulp without breathing. On the recitation, the Medinan readers and 'Asim and Hamza read shurba with a damma, the others with a fatha; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the fatha is the verbal noun and the damma the noun of the act. The word nuzul, in almost all views, is ironic: it normally means the welcome given to a guest, and the commentators see mockery in it. The passage then continues with the argument from the first creation to prove resurrection, which the verse invites the listener to recognise.

This verse, in Surah al-Waqi'a, describes the fate of the people of the left in the Hereafter: after eating from the bitter and repugnant tree of zaqqum until their bellies are full, they drink on top of it boiling water, hamim, in a continuous, insatiable way, like thirsty camels. The commentators agree that this is a warning to those who deny the resurrection and who stray from guidance. They differ over the meaning of al-hiym. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Qatada and al-Dahhak say it refers to camels afflicted with a disease that makes them thirst without ever being quenched, while Ibn 'Abbas in another report, Sufyan al-Thawri and Ibn 'Uyayna take it to mean sand or sandy ground that soaks up water without ever being satisfied. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the second drinking differs from the first, and that the particle fa' signals immediate succession. On the readings of shurb with a damma or a fatha, the linguists largely hold that the fatha is the verbal noun and the damma a noun for the thing drunk. In this context, most commentators read the word nuzul as irony, since it normally denotes the welcome given to a guest.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the description of the food and drink of the people of the left in the Fire. The word nuzul refers to what is prepared for a guest on arrival, and here it is used ironically: this is the welcome awaiting them on the Day of Recompense. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that it is the provision or sustenance set out for them, presented with mockery. The commentators agree that eating from the zaqqum tree, drinking boiling water and drinking like thirsty camels form the punishment prepared for them, and the verse concludes the warning by stating their fate. The main difference concerns the reading of shurb: the people of Medina, Asim and Hamza read it with a damma, the others with a fatha. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the fatha is the verbal noun and the damma a noun meaning the thing drunk, and that both are good usages. On the meaning of al-hiym, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and Qatada take it to mean thirsty camels afflicted with the disease of haym, which stops them from being quenched, while al-Dahhak and Ibn Uyayna take it to mean sandy land that does not hold water. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also report that some understood it as the plural of a thirsty wanderer. The phrase yawm al-din is generally taken to mean the Day of Judgment and recompense. Most commentators do not raise a legal ruling in connection with this verse.

God addresses the disbelievers who denied resurrection with a plain argument: it is He who created them, so why do they not affirm that the One who originated creation can bring it back? Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, take the verse to mean belief in the resurrection, since whoever began creation is all the more able to repeat it. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi allow that the rebuke may concern belief in creation itself: the people acknowledged it, yet their conduct contradicted that belief, so they were treated as deniers. Al-Mawardi offers a different reading, that God created their provision, so why do they not believe that this is their food?

The passage continues with arguments drawn from the creation of man from semen, from the decree of death and from the first creation. Most exegetes understand the first creation as the formation of the human being from a drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh; Qatada and al-Dahhak read it as the creation of Adam. Ibn Kathir explains that the argument answers those who found resurrection unlikely once they had become dust and bones.

On the meaning of the phrase the commentators largely agree. Most treat the verse as a rational proof of resurrection, based on the principle that bringing creation back is no harder than originating it. The commonly accepted sense is therefore an invitation to recognise resurrection from the evidence of the first creation.

God addresses those who deny resurrection with a question meant to bring them to admit the truth: tell Me about the semen you emit into the wombs of women, do you create it as a human being, or are We the Creator? The commentators explain that the aim is to establish God's power to restore life after they have already acknowledged His power to originate it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the obvious answer to be that God is the Creator, while al-Mawardi notes that the verse may also express a favour, the creation of a well-formed human from a base fluid, or a proof that the One who made what is seen can remake what is unseen. On the phrase 'We have decreed death among you', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as a distribution of death, some dying young and others living to old age, al-Dahhak as an equal portion for the inhabitants of heaven and earth, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi as meaning 'decided' or 'written'. For 'We are not outdone', most say that God cannot be overcome or prevented from replacing them, while al-Hasan alone takes the replacement to mean transformation into apes and swine, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab speaks of black birds in Barhut, and Mujahid of whatever form He wills. The passage closes by rebuking those who do not reflect on the first creation, and several scholars cite it as support for reasoning by analogy.

This verse confronts those who deny the Resurrection with something they can see: the seed that they emit into the wombs of their wives. Are you the ones who shape it into a complete human being, or are We the Creator? The commentators agree that God is the Creator, and that the One who began creation can repeat it. Al-Tabari and Mujahid explain that God has decreed death among people, some dying young and some old, while the phrase 'no one can outpace Us' means that no one can go beyond or delay his appointed term. Regarding 'and We will bring you into forms you do not know', Mujahid understands any form God wishes, al-Hasan understands it as transformation into apes and swine as happened to earlier peoples, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab understands it as souls placed in the crops of black birds at Barhut. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the verse contains an argument by analogy, since God reproaches the deniers for not reasoning from the first creation to the second. Al-Razi observes that the question about the seed establishes an uncaused Creator who ends the chain of causes. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress the same point: the One who began creation can bring it back. The verse thus rests on an observable fact to prove resurrection, and the commentators differ mainly on the meaning of the future forms and on the readings of the verbs 'qaddarna' and 'tamunna'.

In this verse God states that He has decreed death among people, and that no one can outrun Him or prevent it. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Qurtubi, understand that God apportioned death among people with different terms, so that some die as children, others as young people and others in old age. Al-Dahhak, followed by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, reads the word as meaning that God made death equal for all, so that no one is spared. The phrase 'we are not outpaced' is explained by most as meaning that God is not defeated or overcome, a reading found in al-Jalalayn, al-Alusi and Ibn Kathir. Al-Tabari connects the words 'on condition that' to the decree itself, meaning that God causes one generation to die so that another may replace it, while most others attach it to God's power to replace people. As for 'in what you do not know', al-Hasan takes it to mean transformation into apes and swine, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab into black birds in Barhut, Mujahid into whatever form God wills, and many others into changed attributes at the resurrection. Nearly all conclude that the verse proves the possibility of resurrection, since the One who created you the first time can recreate you, as al-Razi and Ibn Kathir stress. Ibn Atiyya also reports that some scholars cite it as evidence for the validity of analogical reasoning.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the Qur'an's proofs of resurrection. God states that He has decreed death among people with differing terms, that no one can outrun it or escape it, and that He is able to replace the addressees with others like them and to bring them into being in a form or state they do not know. Most agree that 'qaddarna' means that God decreed, prescribed or apportioned death, and that 'ma nahnu bi-masbuqin' means that no one overcomes or frustrates Him. Regarding 'nubaddila amthalakum', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari take it as the destruction of people and their replacement by similar ones, which shows God's power to raise them again. For 'wa-nunshi'akum fima la ta'lamun', Mujahid understands any form God wills, al-Hasan a transformation into apes and swine, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab bodies inside the crops of black birds at Barhut, and as-Suddi a creation other than their own. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer resurrection with attributes unknown to them. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the threat dominates the verse and reports al-Hasan in that sense. Al-Razi notes that life and death are under God's will and that the verse confirms His power to restore life. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that 'amthalakum' means the resurrection itself and that the first creation proves the second. All of them note that the verse ends by calling people to remember the first creation so that they reflect and take heed.

The commentators explain that this verse reminds people that they know their first creation, meaning their coming into being after having been nothing, and rebukes them for not reflecting on it. Most of them take this to mean the formation of the human being from a drop of semen, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, as stated by Mujahid, al-Kalbi, Muqatil and al-Tabari. Others, including Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir, understand it as the creation of Adam from clay. The general sense is an argument by analogy: whoever could create once can recreate. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi draw from it a proof of the validity of analogical reasoning, while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur restrict its force to an argument a fortiori from a known beginning. The readings differ on the word al-nash'a, pronounced with a short or long vowel, and on tadhakkarun, read with or without doubling, and the commentators do not settle between them. Ibn Ashur observes that the present tense leaves the door of reflection still open. All agree that the aim is to urge people to reflect on their first creation in order to infer the resurrection, in connection with the signs mentioned just after: the semen, the sown field, the water and the fire.

This verse asks the addressees, in a rhetorical challenge, about the tilling in which they turn the soil and cast the seed: do they make it grow into a crop, or is it God who causes it to sprout? The commentators agree that the growth is God's act alone, and that human action ends with ploughing and sowing. Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that tilling means breaking the soil and scattering seed, while growing means God making it sprout. Al-Qurtubi, citing al-Mawardi, mentions the report from Abu Hurayra that one should say "I have tilled" rather than "I have sown", which al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also transmit, although al-Bayhaqi judges it weak. Al-Razi and al-Mawardi use the verse as evidence for resurrection: the One who brings a plant out of a decayed seed can restore the dead. The next verses suppose God could turn the harvest into dry chaff, leaving the listeners astonished. The commentators differ on the meaning of "tafakkahun": Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it as wonder, al-Hasan as regret, Ikrima as mutual blame, Ibn Zayd as lamentation, and al-Kisa'i treats it as one of the words with opposite meanings. On "innA lamughramun", Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas read it as "tormented", Mujahid as "infatuated" and al-Dahhak as "ruined", while "bal nahnu mahrumun" means being deprived of provision. The passage thus recalls the blessing of grain and offers a proof of the resurrection.

In this verse God asks people about the seed they plant in the ground: do they make it grow and bring it to maturity, or is it God alone who does so? The commentators explain that ploughing and sowing are the work of people, while the growth of the plant belongs to God. Some, such as Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, cite a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ advising people to say "I have tilled" rather than "I have sown", though Ibn Kathir notes that some of its chains are weak. The commentators agree that the verse demonstrates God's power to raise the dead, since the One who makes the seed sprout after it has disappeared can also bring people back to life. The passage goes on to say that, if God willed, He would turn the crop into dry chaff, and people would be astonished, grieved or reproach one another, saying, "We are burdened with debt" or "we are deprived". On the meaning of "tafakkahun", Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it as wonder, al-Hasan and Qatada as regret, Ikrima as mutual blame, and Ibn Kaysan as sorrow. On "mughramun", Qatada understands it as "tormented", Mujahid as "attached to us". Al-Tabari prefers the sense of wonder as closest to the context. The following verses recall the blessings of water and fire, before God orders the Prophet to glorify the name of his Lord.

This passage in Surah al-Waqi'a shows that the harvest, which God causes to grow and protects, is a favour from Him: had He willed, He would have turned it into dry stubble from which no one benefits. On the phrase ﴿فَظَلْتُمْ تَفَكَّهُونَ﴾, the most widely reported meaning, from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada and preferred by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, is that you marvel at what befell your crops. Al-Hasan and Qatada, in one report, take it to mean regret over the expenses or the sins committed, Ikrima takes it as blaming one another, and Ibn Kaysan as grief. Some philologists, such as al-Kisa'i, note that the verb is one of the words with opposite meanings, signifying both delight and sorrow.

Regarding ﴿إِنَّا لَمُغْرَمُونَ﴾, most explain it as "tormented" or "ruined", citing verses where the word means punishment. Mujahid and Ikrima understand it as "attached to us", while Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Kaysan read it as the loss of wealth for nothing in return. Finally, ﴿بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ﴾ is generally taken as deprivation of provision, meaning being destitute and without good fortune.

The commentators link the verse to the argument for resurrection, since the One who makes the seed grow can recreate living beings. All agree that it reminds people of God's favour and calls them to gratitude.

This verse describes the words of the deniers of resurrection: had God willed, He would have turned their sown field into dry, useless stubble, so that they would wonder at the loss, speak to one another about it, and say, "We are ruined." The commentators agree that the verse is an argument for God's power and for resurrection, and that God alone makes the seed grow. On the word "tafakkahun", al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report the meaning "you marvel", transmitted from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, while Ikrima takes it as "you blame one another", al-Hasan and Qatada as "you regret", and Ibn Kaysan as "you grieve". Al-Kisa'i holds that the word is one of those with opposite meanings, so it may also mean to be pleased. For "inna la-mughramun", al-Tabari, appealing to Arabic poetic usage, chooses "we are being punished", as Qatada and Ibn Abbas explain, whereas Mujahid and Ikrima take it as "we are infatuated with it", Ibn Kaysan as "we have lost our wealth", and Muqatil as "we are destroyed". Finally, "bal nahnu mahrumun" means, according to Mujahid and Qatada, that we are deprived of provision and good fortune, having neither luck nor prosperity.

This passage from Surat al-Waqi'a reminds people of the blessing of the harvest. If God willed, He would turn the field they have ploughed into dry stubble, and they would be left in distress and bewilderment; they would say, "We are burdened with debt", that is, tormented or saddled with the expenses they incurred, "nay, we are deprived" of our livelihood. The commentators agree on the general sense: it describes the condition of those whose crops have been struck by disaster. The word "tafakkahun" is interpreted in different ways. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, followed by al-Hasan, read it as "you marvel"; 'Ikrima reads it as "you blame one another"; al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi as "you regret"; Ibn Kaysan as "you grieve"; and al-Kisa'i regards it as a word with opposite meanings. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of wonder, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the root signifies the loss of joy and cheerfulness, which points to sadness. As for "mughramun", Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas read it as "tormented", 'Ikrima and Mujahid as "devoted to us", Mujahid also as "exposed to evil", and al-Dahhak as "having lost their wealth"; al-Tabari adopts the sense of torment. "Mahrumun" means for Mujahid and Qatada those deprived of luck and gain. The commentators link this verse to the affirmation that God alone makes the crop grow, and a tradition from Abu Hurayra asks people to say "I have ploughed" rather than "I have sown". Ibn Sa'di sees in the verse a call to gratitude towards God for the harvests He makes grow.

God asks people about the water they drink: did they bring it down from the clouds themselves, or is He the one who sends it down? Most commentators understand al-muzn as the clouds. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it to mean the clouds, while Ibn Abbas and al-Thawri add the sky, and al-Zamakhshari reports that it may refer only to the white clouds, whose water is the sweetest. They agree on the general meaning: a reminder of the blessing of sweet water fit for drinking. Had God willed, He would have made it salty and bitter, unfit for drinking or irrigation, which calls for gratitude. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi connect this passage to what precedes it, the sowing and the fire, to stress God's power and favours. Al-Razi explains that water is mentioned after food because a blessing is complete only with eating and drinking, and that gratitude is more evident here since man has no part in the water's descent. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur note that drink follows food, which explains the order of the verses. Ibn Uthaymin and al-Jaza'iri add that the water originates in the clouds and that God channels it into springs beneath the earth. Ibn Ashur also sees here an argument for resurrection. The commentators do not disagree on the core meaning, only on the precise definition of muzn and on how the verse links to its context.

In this verse God addresses people about the sweet water they drink and asks whether they brought it down from the clouds or whether He is the one who sends it down. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir, explain that al-muzn means the clouds, singular muznah, though Ibn Abbas is also reported to have said it means both sky and cloud, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that some take it to mean specifically the white cloud, whose water is the sweetest. They explain that had God willed, He would have made this water salty and bitter, unfit for drinking or irrigation, and so the verse calls for gratitude. All of them agree that the verse affirms God's power and oneness and reminds people of His favour. Ibn 'Ashur links the passage to the proof of resurrection, since God brings into being from nothing what gives life. The commentators also explain why the emphatic particle appears before the verse on food but not before the verse on drink: al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy see this as showing that food takes precedence, since drink follows it, while al-Razi gives another reason based on the act of drinking being part of enjoying the blessing. The following verses concern the fire that is struck from wood. Most exegetes read it as a reminder of the fire of Hell. Al-Mawardi and most others take al-muqwin to mean travellers, though others say the hungry or anyone who benefits from fire.

The commentators explain that the verse reminds people of the blessing of water: God sends it down from the clouds, and if He willed, He could make it salty and bitter, unfit for drinking or for irrigation, so gratitude is due for this favour. Ibn Abbas understood ajaj as intensely salty, while al-Hasan took it as bitter, and some took it as scalding and corrosive. Most, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Tabari, take muzn to mean clouds, although Ibn Abbas and al-Thawri add the sky. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Ashur note that the emphatic lam, present in the verse on crops but absent here, is dropped for brevity, the food being given prominence over drink, which follows from it. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that the word for gratitude is used because water is pure bounty with no human labour involved, and that a blessing is complete only when one both eats and drinks. Ibn Ashur sees the verse as an argument from God's power to strip water of its usefulness, a prelude to urging gratitude and rejecting polytheism. Ibn Kathir also cites hadiths about giving thanks when drinking water.

This verse asks people about the fire they strike from the firestick. The commentators agree that God created the tree from which it comes, and that the fire is a sign of His power. On the meaning of the tree, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and Mujahid, as cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, identify it as the marikh and ifar, two woods whose branches are rubbed together to produce sparks, while Qatada and al-Zajjaj take it to be the wood that is rubbed, and Ibn Ashur explains the same. A minority, mentioned by Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Atiyya, read the tree as the fire itself, which Ibn Atiyya judges to be a strained reading. Concerning the phrase 'a reminder', Qatada, Mujahid and Ikrima take it to mean a reminder of the great fire of Hell, Mujahid adding that it gives light in darkness, and Ata' taking it as an admonition for the believer.

The phrase 'a provision for the muqwin' has several readings. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Tabari hold that the muqwin are travellers who dwell in desert wastes, a view al-Tabari supports with verse, while Mujahid understands all people who benefit from fire for cooking and warmth, whether travelling or settled. Ibn Zayd takes them to be the hungry, and Qutrub notes that the word has opposite meanings, poor or rich. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi stress that the travellers benefit most, since they rely on fire for light and warmth at night.

In this verse God draws attention to the fire that people produce by striking a flint and tinder, asking: did you cause the tree from which it comes to grow, or are We the Producers? The commentators agree on the core meaning: humans do not create the tree of fire; God alone brings it into being. Most identify this tree as the mirkh and the 'iffar, whose green branches the Arabs rubbed together until sparks flew. Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya suggest that the word 'tree' may refer to the firestick itself, while Ibn Jarir and others take it to be the tree, and some point to iron or the root of the tree. All agree that God made this fire a reminder (tadhkira) of the Hellfire, as Qatada, Mujahid and 'Ikrima report, and a hadith is cited that the fire of this world is one part of seventy of the fire of Hell. The phrase 'a provision for the muqwin' is where the views diverge most. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jarir take it to mean travellers crossing empty desert; Mujahid includes both travellers and residents who benefit from it; Ibn Zayd understands the hungry; and Qutrub, treating the word as one of those with opposite meanings, includes both the poor and the rich. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir chiefly favour the sense of travellers, while recognising that the verse's wider scope covers all these benefits.

This verse states that God made the fire kindled from wood a reminder of the fire of Hell and a comfort for the "muqwin". The commentators largely agree that the worldly fire recalls the greater fire of the Hereafter. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take it as a reminder of the greater fire, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that the fire of this world is one part in seventy of the fire of Hell. The meaning of "muqwin" is more disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak, whom al-Tabari also prefers as the strongest view, understand travellers who camp in empty desert. Mujahid and Ikrima include both travellers and residents who benefit from the fire. Ibn Zayd takes it to mean the hungry, and Qutrub, who counts the word among those with opposite meanings, applies it to both the poor and the rich.

Al-Samarqandi and al-Baghawi explain that travellers are singled out because they gain most from fire: warmth, light, protection from wild animals, and guidance on the road at night. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that mentioning travellers reminds the reader that all of this worldly life is a journey. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the word can combine both senses, traveller and hungry, since their need for fire is especially pressing.

The commentators draw no legal rulings from this verse. They read it as evidence of God's power, who produces fire from green wood, and as a sign that should lead the mind to the Day of Judgment.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to glorify the name of his Lord, the Mighty, that is, to declare Him far above every imperfection and to exalt Him in gratitude for the signs of His power and the blessings just listed. The commentators agree that the particle fa links the command to the preceding verses, which argue for resurrection from the evidence of creation, the sown seed, water and fire. They differ on the sense of the preposition bi in bismi. Ibn Kathir, al-Jaza'iri and Ibn 'Ashur take it as a particle of attachment or accompaniment, meaning glorify while invoking the name of your Lord, whereas al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari regard the word name as superfluous or as meaning remembrance. Ibn al-Qayyim holds that the glorification must be made with both heart and tongue. Several scholars, among them al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Uthaymin, report that the formula is to say Glory be to my Lord the Mighty, and that the Prophet ﷺ instructed that it be recited in bowing (ruku'). As for the epithet al-'Azim, some attach it to the Lord and others to the name, and the commentators do not choose between these readings. The verse thus closes the argument for resurrection with a call to glorify God against the denial of the disbelievers.

This verse swears by the positions of the stars, which most commentators understand as their setting places in the sky, a view held by Qatada and Mujahid and preferred by al-Tabari, and it stresses that this oath is of a magnitude people do not fully grasp. The commentators differ over the particle la before the verb: most, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, treat it as an emphatic addition meaning I swear; others, such as al-Farra' and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, read it as a negation that rebuts the claims of the disbelievers about the Quran, and some take it as a denial of swearing at all because the matter is too clear to need one. As for the stars, there are two main readings: Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid and others say they are the stars of the Quran, revealed in portions, while Ibn Kathir and the majority say they are the heavenly bodies; al-Dahhak linked them to the anwa', the star-risings to which pre-Islamic Arabs attributed rain. The sworn content is that the Quran is generous, meaning of great worth and benefit, and that it is in a hidden book, which Ibn Abbas and Jabir ibn Zayd took to be the Preserved Tablet, Ikrima took to be the Torah and the Gospel, and Mujahid and Qatada took to be the codex in our hands. On the verse that only the purified touch it, most scholars take the purified to be the angels; Qatada, Malik and others apply it to the rule on touching the mushaf, and a letter attributed to the Prophet required ritual purity for touching the Quran, while Ibn Abbas and al-Sha'bi allowed it for the minor impurity. Al-Farra' reads it as meaning only believers taste its benefit.

This verse swears by the positions of the stars. For most exegetes these are their setting points and places of setting. Some took the particle la as an emphatic addition, meaning I swear, while others took it as a negation rejecting what the disbelievers say about the Qur'an. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others note that the oath by the stars is great and deserves honour. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid and al-Suddi understood the stars as the Qur'an's revealed portions, sent down in stages. Al-Hasan took them to be their scattering and falling on the Day of Judgement, and al-Dahhak identified them with the seasonal constellations to which the pre-Islamic Arabs attributed rain. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn al-Qayyim favour the interpretation as the stars and their setting, since the word nujum generally refers to the heavenly bodies in the Qur'an. The clause "and it is indeed a great oath, if you only knew" is a parenthesis that all commentators agree magnifies the oath, and some supply the answer "you would have glorified it". What is sworn to is that the Qur'an is noble, meaning excellent, beneficial and honourable. As for "in a Book well guarded", Ibn Abbas and most scholars take it as the Preserved Tablet, while Mujahid and Qatada take it as the codex in our hands. On "which none touch but the purified", most say the angels are meant, while others say people purified from major and minor impurity or from sin. Some jurists have used this verse to forbid touching the mushaf without ablution, but others hold that it does not establish this, since the passage is a rebuke addressed to those who deny the Qur'an.

God swears by the positions of the stars, meaning their settings or their stations, to stress the greatness of this oath, and then declares that the Qur'an being recited is a noble, excellent book of great benefit, which the commentators tie to its guidance, clarity and wisdom. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take the particle in "fa-la" as an emphatic addition, so the sense is "I swear"; others, including al-Farra' and Ibn Juzayy, read it as a negation that rejects the claims of the disbelievers. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi understand the positions of the stars as the Qur'an's stars, sent down in stages; al-Hasan takes them as their scattering on the Day of Resurrection; and al-Dahhak as the star-attributed rains of pre-Islamic custom.

The "Book kept hidden" is, for Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Qayyim, the Preserved Tablet or the scripture held by the angels; Ikrima takes it to be the Torah and the Gospel, while Mujahid and Qatada take it to be the codex in our hands. As for "which none touch but the purified", most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir, identify them as the angels; others understand those free from ritual impurity, an argument juristic schools use to bar those in a state of impurity from touching the mushaf. Al-Farra' reads it as meaning that only believers taste its benefit, and al-Qasimi notes that the disputed report of Amr ibn Hazm supports the legal view.

The revelation is finally described as a descent from the Lord of the worlds, in answer to those who claimed it was the work of devils.

God swears by the positions of the stars, meaning their setting places and their stations, to stress the greatness of this oath, and then affirms that the Qur'an is noble, meaning abundant in benefit, rich in good and high in rank, and that it is in a Book that is guarded and hidden. The commentators differ about this Book: Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it to be the Preserved Tablet or a Book in heaven, 'Ikrima says the Torah and the Gospel, al-Suddi the Psalms, while Mujahid and Qatada identify it with the codex in our hands, and Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Juzayy think of the scrolls held by the angels. As for 'none touch it but the purified', most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand the angels, while Qatada, al-Kalbi and al-Rabi' ibn Anas speak of purity from ritual impurity or sin, and al-Farra' of those who believe. Some jurists cite this verse to forbid touching the mushaf in a state of ritual impurity, but the commentators do not decide between these readings.

God swears by the positions of the stars, meaning their setting places or their mansions, to stress the greatness of this oath, and then affirms that the Qur'an is noble, in a protected Book hidden from creatures. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, hold that this hidden Book is the one in heaven and that those who touch it are the purified angels, so the verse means that demons cannot reach it. Abu al-'Aliya and Ibn Zayd understand the purified as messengers cleansed of sin among angels and humans. 'Ikrima takes the Book to be the Torah and the Gospel, while Mujahid and Qatada take it to be the mushaf in our hands. On that reading, scholars differ on the meaning of touching: Qatada, al-Kalbi and al-Rabi' ibn Anas understand the purified as those cleansed from ritual impurity, polytheism or sins, while al-Farra' holds that only believers taste its benefit. Most jurists, including Malik, al-Shafi'i, 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, rely on this verse and on the Prophet's letter to 'Amr ibn Hazm to forbid touching the mushaf in a state of minor impurity, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi and Dawud permit it, and Malik grants leniency to children and teachers. The commentators also note that the verse answers those who claimed that devils had brought the Qur'an, and affirms that it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that the Qur'an is a revelation sent down from the Lord of the worlds, and that it is neither the speech of a human being nor the words of a soothsayer or poet, as the polytheists claimed. Most understand the word tanzil as meaning 'that which has been sent down': the verbal noun stands in the place of the passive participle, as noted by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi. The word is read in the nominative, making it a qualifier of the Qur'an or the predicate of an implied subject, and in the accusative, making it an object or adverbial complement.

Most exegetes link the verse to what precedes it: naming the Lord of the worlds reinforces the sanctity of the preserved Book. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that lordship implies that God does not leave His creatures without guidance, and he considers this argument from the divine attributes stronger than the argument from miracles. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the Qur'an comes from that preserved Book, and they also connect the passage to the refutation of those who claimed that devils had brought it.

Opinions differ on the identity of the 'Hidden Book': Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima and Ibn Jubayr take it to be the heavenly Book or the Preserved Tablet, while Qatada and Mujahid identify it with the codex in our hands. Ikrima also mentions the Torah and the Gospel. The commentators report these views without choosing between them.

This verse rebukes the disbelievers for being lenient toward the Qur'an and for going easy on those who reject it. Most commentators read the word mudhinun as meaning deniers: Ibn Abbas, Muqatil, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir all take it this way, while Mujahid understands it as colluding with the disbelievers in their unbelief, al-Dahhak as turning away, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan as negligence or lack of earnestness in accepting the Qur'an. The next verse is read almost unanimously as a rebuke to those who attribute rain to the stars: the word rizq is taken to mean thanks, so that gratitude is replaced by denial. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi cite readings attributed to Ali and Ibn Abbas, "your thanks", and the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid about rain attributed to stars. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy hold that the prohibition concerns believing that a star causes the rain, not merely using seasonal markers, a distinction that al-Shafi'i is also reported to have drawn. Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Razi and al-Qasimi also see here a description of the Qur'an as a living source of life for the soul, so that rejecting it amounts to making denial one's nourishment. The commentators differ on what the Preserved Book is and who the purified are, but the overall meaning is clear: the word of God must not be treated with compromise.

The commentators read this verse as a rebuke addressed to those who dealt with the Qur'an in a lax or dismissive way. Ibn Abbas, cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, explains that the phrase 'afa-bihadha al-hadith antum mudhinun' means that you deny it, while al-Mujahid takes it as colluding with the disbelievers. For the second clause, 'wa tajalun rizqakum annakum tukadhdhibun', the majority reading makes it: you put denial in place of thanks for your provision. Ali and Ibn Abbas read 'shukrakum' (your gratitude), a reading al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi also report. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that most of the reports concern people who said 'we were given rain by such-and-such a star', and they cite the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, in which one who credits the rain to God's mercy is a believer, while one who credits it to a star is a disbeliever. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baghawi understand 'rizq' here as the rain. Al-Hasan al-Basri takes it as one's share of the Qur'an, which for those who receive only denial is a loss. Al-Razi offers a further reading: people may make their livelihood the denial of the Prophet, out of fear of losing their gains, though he notes that most exegetes adopt the first meaning. Ibn Atiyya reports the consensus that the verse rebukes those who attributed rain to the stars.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the rebuke of those who deny the Qur'an and attribute their rain to the stars. God says: why then, when the soul reaches the throat at the moment of death, while you are present and watching the dying person, do you not bring it back? God is closer to him than you are, by His knowledge and power, or through His angels who take the soul, but you do not see them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that nafs means the soul, that the hulqum is the passage of breath and food, and that the address is to the dying person's family and all who are present. Being unable to hold the soul back shows that the matter lies beyond human control. The scholars differ on the phrase 'not held to account': Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Ata, Ikrima, al-Hasan and Qatada take it to mean not judged or recompensed, Mujahid means not certain, while al-Farra and Ibn Qutayba understand it as not subjugated or dominated. Al-Mawardi lists seven interpretations. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim explain that both conditional clauses share one answer, 'you would bring it back', as al-Farra held. Ibn Ashur stresses that the soul is taken only so that it may be recompensed, which completes the argument. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya propose a different word order that leaves the overall meaning unchanged.

The commentators explain that this verse, in the context of death, means that when the soul reaches the throat at the moment of agony, those present watch the dying person without being able to ward off what has befallen him. The address is general to all who attend the deathbed, according to al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir. Ibn Kathir and others take the nearness to be that of the angels who take the soul, while al-Tabari and al-Baghawi also mention nearness by God's knowledge and power. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Alusi note that seeing may be with the eyes if the angels are meant, or with the heart if God is meant.

The commentators agree that the following verses establish human helplessness before death, and that this helplessness shows the matter lies with God. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim see it as an argument against those who deny resurrection, since they cannot return the soul once it has reached the throat. The conditional clause 'if you are not subject to judgment' receives the same answer as the first condition, 'you would bring it back', as al-Farra' is cited as saying. The meaning of 'mudinin' divides them: al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari take it as 'not subject to a ruler', while Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan take it as 'not judged or recompensed', the most widespread reading.

The exegetes therefore agree on the core meaning: a reminder of death and of divine power. Their differences concern the nature of the nearness, the sense of seeing, and the precise meaning of 'mudinin', and none disputes the general scope of the verse.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage rebuking the disbelievers: when the soul reaches the throat at the moment of death, those present cannot bring it back, and God is nearer to the dying person than they are. On the nature of this nearness, opinions differ. Ibn Abbas, Abu Salih, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the angels who receive the soul, while al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Razi, as well as al-Shawkani, al-Qasimi and Abu al-Su'ud, understand God's nearness through His knowledge, power and control. Ibn Juzayy notes both readings. The clause 'you do not see' is also read two ways: most say it means the angels are not perceived, while others say it means the bystanders do not grasp what is happening to the dying person. On the phrase 'not subject to judgment', the scholars vary: Ibn Abbas and most early exegetes take it as 'not recompensed', al-Hasan and Qatada as 'not resurrected', Mujahid as 'not certain', and al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba as 'not owned or subjugated'. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur consider the sense of being recompensed the most apt. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from the verse the argument that the inability to restore the soul proves that a Lord controls mankind. The commentators do not weigh between these views and present them all.

These verses describe the moment of death: when the soul reaches the throat and the bystanders watch helplessly, God is nearer to the dying person through His knowledge, power and angels. He then asks the deniers why they do not return the soul, if they are not subject to judgment and recompense. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Hasan explain 'not subject to judgment' as 'not called to account and not repaid for deeds', while al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to mean 'not believing in resurrection', Mujahid 'not certain', and al-Farra' 'not subjugated'. The commentators agree that the two conditions share one answer, and that the inability to bring back the soul shows that the matter belongs to God alone. The verses then describe three states: those brought near receive rest, comfort and a Garden of bliss, the people of the right are greeted with peace, and the denying deviators receive boiling water and the blazing fire. On the meaning of 'rawh' and 'rayhan' opinions differ: Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take 'rawh' as joy, Mujahid as rest, and al-Dahhak as forgiveness; Mujahid and Sa'id take 'rayhan' as provision, while Abu al-'Aliya describes a fragrant plant brought to the dying person. Al-Tabari prefers that 'rawh' means joy and mercy, and 'rayhan' the plant offered at death. The majority read 'farawhun' with a fatha, while al-Hasan and 'A'isha read it with a damma. The commentators present the passage as an affirmation of resurrection, recompense and the truth of the Qur'an.

These verses describe the moment of death, when the soul reaches the throat and those present cannot bring it back, a reminder that its fate is not in their hands. Most commentators explain the phrase "not held to account" as meaning not repaid for deeds nor called to reckoning, so the sense is: if you are free of any reckoning or recompense, why do you not return the soul? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take this view, and al-Tabari judges it the most correct. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read it as "not believing in resurrection", Mujahid as "not certain", Maymun ibn Mihran as "not subjugated", and al-Farra' as "not owned". Most scholars treat the repeated "law la" as sharing one answer, "you would return it", as in the verse about guidance coming from Him. On the rewards of those brought near, the majority reads "rawh" with a fatha, meaning rest, joy or forgiveness, while al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'isha read it with a damma, meaning life or mercy. Mujahid takes "rayhan" as provision, while Abu al-'Aliya takes it as the fragrant herb held to the dying person, the sense al-Tabari prefers. All agree the passage divides people at death into three groups, with the deniers and the astray receiving boiling water and the blaze.

This part of the verse describes the state of the deceased if he is among the near-brought, the foremost in good deeds, as Abu al-Aliya and Ibn 'Atiyya explain. The general meaning most commentators give is that he receives rawh, rayhan and the garden of bliss: rest, a pleasant provision and lasting delight. On the word rawh, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir understand repose and relief from the worldly life, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid joy and ease, al-Hasan and Qatada mercy and forgiveness, and others deliverance from the Fire. On rayhan, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as sustenance, while Abu al-Aliya and al-Hasan take it as the known fragrant plant, a sprig from the garden of Paradise that the near-brought smells before his soul is taken; al-Tabari considers this the most apparent meaning. There is also a difference of recitation: most read fa-rawhun with a fatha, whereas Ya'qub, Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'isha read fa-ruhun with a damma. Al-Hasan explains this form as the soul leaving amid the fragrance, Qatada and Ibn Qutayba as mercy or lasting life, and al-Zajjaj as an eternal life without death. Some link this favour to the moment of death, others to the Hereafter, and Ibn Kathir judges these views close and all valid, the near-brought receiving all of them.

This passage describes the state of three groups at the moment of death, after a renewed argument for resurrection. For the near ones, the foremost in goodness, there is "rest and fragrance" and a Garden of delight. Commentators differ on the meaning of these words. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Dahhak explain "rest" as relief or joy, sometimes as forgiveness and mercy, and "fragrance" as provision or repose. Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya and Qatada take the fragrance to be a sweet-smelling plant that the soul is said to leave while it is smelled. The reading "furuh" with a damma, attributed to 'A'isha and to the Prophet, was understood by some as mercy or an enduring life. The Garden of delight is the promised Paradise, shown to the dying person. For the people of the right there is "peace": some read it as safety from punishment, others as the greeting of the angels who inform them of their rank, or of the people of Paradise. For the denying, misguided ones there is a welcome of boiling water and burning in the Hellfire. The commentators agree that this account is the certainty of truth, and that the verse ends with a command to glorify the name of the Mighty Lord. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that this was later linked to glorifying God in bowing during prayer.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the description of souls at the moment of death, and that the companions of the right form the second category, those who fulfilled the obligations and avoided the forbidden. The meaning of 'Peace be upon you from the companions of the right' is, for most, a promise of safety: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the angels greet him and tell him he is among the companions of the right, while Qatada and Ibn Zayd understand it as deliverance from Allah's punishment. Al-Baghawi and al-Zajjaj see instead a message to the Prophet, who should not worry about them. Al-Farra' explains that the sense is: it is granted to you that they are among the companions of the right, a reading al-Bukhari also reports.

Al-Razi gives several readings: the companions of the right greet one another, or the verse means that tranquility is secured, or it expresses the high rank of these people. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that this is not a greeting of courtesy but good news of security at the moment of departure from this world. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a summary closing of the surah, returning to the three categories in reverse order.

The commentators agree that the companions of the right stand below the foremost, and that they enjoy safety in contrast with the fate of the deniers and the astray, who receive boiling water and the blaze. Several, including Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari, link these verses to the moment of dying. They differ mainly on who gives the greeting and on the exact scope of the formula.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the description of the three groups of people at death and at judgement. Its plain sense is that the people of the right are granted safety and deliverance from punishment. Al-Tabari and al-Farra' read the phrase "fa-salamun laka min ashab al-yamin" as meaning "peace is yours, you who are among the people of the right," with some taking an elided particle in the sentence. Ibn Kathir reports that the angels greet the dying person and tell him he is among the people of the right, a view that Qatada and Ibn Zayd share, adding that God and His angels send him greetings. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention greeting from God or the angels. Al-Razi gives three meanings: one person of the right greets another, the person is granted safety from a matter that frightened his heart, or the phrase conveys the high rank of these people. He also considers that the address may be to the Prophet, who need fear nothing for them; Ibn Juzayy and Abu al-Su'ud adopt this reading. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya list the same possibilities without deciding among them. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the verse gives the departing soul glad tidings of safety rather than a greeting. The commentators do not choose between these readings and present them as meanings the context allows.

The commentators explain that this verse completes the description of the three groups of people at death and afterwards, and here it names the third group, the deniers who have gone astray. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi say that they will have a nuzul, meaning what is offered to a guest, namely boiling water that has reached the extreme of its heat, and a tasliya in the blaze, meaning being burned by the fire. Ibn 'Atiyya explains that these are the disbelievers, the people of the left and of the unfavourable side, and that the nuzul is what is first served to a visitor, while tasliya means direct contact with the fire. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi likewise identify this group as the disbelievers. Al-Razi observes that denial is mentioned first here because the punishment is tied to its cause, unlike the wording in verse fifty-one. Al-Zamakhshari reads the word nuzul as sarcasm. The commentators agree that this recompense is a certainty, haqq al-yaqin. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that some place this fate at the moment of death, and others at the Day of Resurrection. The surah ends with the command to glorify the name of the Great Lord, and al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the Prophet asked that it be recited in bowing, though the chains of transmission of this report are debated.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the description of people's fate at the moment of death. It speaks of those who denied the truth and went astray: for them there is a "nuzul", the welcome offered to a guest on arrival, which is "hamim", water heated to an extreme temperature, followed by "tasliyat jahim", being cast into the blazing fire and burned by it. Most agree that "nuzul" is used ironically, a mock hospitality, and that the hamim is scalding water they are made to drink. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand the tasliya as being driven into the fire, while al-Qurtubi and others take it as dwelling in the blaze and suffering its various torments. Al-Alusi reports that some link the scene to what the dead person feels in the grave, the heat and smoke of the fire, while others place it on the Day of Resurrection. Abu Hayyan notes that Abu 'Amr reads "tasliyati" in the genitive, making it depend on "hamim", whereas the majority reading puts it in the nominative, coordinated with "nuzul". These differences concern mainly the timing and nature of this punishment, not the general meaning of the verse.

This verse describes the fate of the dying according to their rank. The near ones, the foremost in faith, receive rest, provision and the Garden of bliss; the people of the right receive peace, meaning safety from punishment; and the misguided deniers have as their hospitality boiling water and the burning of the Blaze. The commentators explain that tasliya means being burned or cast into the fire, and that Jahim is one of the names of the Fire.

Most exegetes agree that the verse divides people into three categories at the moment of death. They differ, however, on the meaning of rawh. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as rest and relief, Ibn Kathir adding mercy, joy and good provision, while Ibn al-Jawzi lists six views, including joy, forgiveness and release from distress. Al-Hasan holds that rayhan is a fragrant plant in which the soul is taken, whereas Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas take it to mean provision.

The reading fa-ruhun with a damma on the ra is attributed to 'A'isha, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, who understood it as mercy. As for the greeting to the people of the right, al-Tabari reads it as safety from punishment, Ibn Kathir as greetings from the angels, and al-Razi allows that the address may be to the Prophet as consolation. The commentators present these explanations as complementary, and none of them settles the matter as definitive.

This verse affirms that what Surat al-Waqi'a has described about people's states at death and in the Hereafter is the established truth beyond any doubt, the certainty of certainty. The commentators explain the construction 'haqq al-yaqin' in different ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean the true report or the certain account. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see it as an emphatic form, like saying 'this is the very certainty', meaning its utmost limit. Al-Razi notes that the construction may rest on an omitted noun or on the sense of 'from'. As for the command to glorify the name of your Lord, the Great, al-Tabari explains it as naming God by His most beautiful names, while Ibn al-Jawzi and others take it to mean prayer and remembrance of the Lord. Some hold that the particle 'bi' is superfluous. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir that this verse should be recited in bowing (ruku'). The commentators do not choose between these views and present them as readings the text can bear.

In this closing verse God commands His Prophet to glorify the name of his Lord, the Mighty, meaning to declare Him free of anything unworthy of His majesty, after affirming that what has been described about the three groups at death and afterwards is the true certainty, beyond doubt. The commentators agree that the verse concludes what precedes it, and that glorification means exalting God and praising Him. They differ on the particle bi: many, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, treat it as redundant so that the sense is glorify the name of your Lord, while others take it as indicating accompaniment, that is glorify Him by mentioning His name, and some as indicating the object. Al-Razi and others note that the name may stand for the divine essence itself. On the phrase haqq al-yaqin, the Basran grammarians read it as an ellipsis meaning the true certainty of the matter, while the Kufans and al-Mubarrad treat it as an annexation of a thing to itself for emphasis, which Ibn 'Atiyya regards as intensification. Qatada holds that God leaves no one without bringing him face to face with the certainty of this Quran: the believer benefits from what he was certain of in this life, whereas the unbeliever becomes certain only when it no longer helps him. Many cite the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir that the Prophet ordered this verse to be recited in bowing, which jurists took as the basis for the prayer formula. Some link the passage to turning away from the words of the disbelievers and devoting oneself to worship and invocation.
